stories.title: Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur says 'everything went wrong' as the team fumbles a Hungarian GP it should have won
stories.what_happened: Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur said "everything went wrong" for the team at Sunday's Hungarian Grand Prix, a race Ferrari had entered with real hope of a strong result given the circuit suited its car. Instead, both Ferrari drivers missed the podium: Charles Leclerc finished 4th and Lewis Hamilton 5th, with Vasseur cataloguing a string of unforced errors — a weak start, a penalty, being passed on-track by Max Verstappen, and pit stops that were consistently **0.2 to 0.3 seconds** slower than they should have been, costing positions each time. Vasseur was blunt that the team's execution, not raw car pace, was the problem on the day. The comments land just as the sport heads into its summer break, giving Ferrari's engineers and strategists several weeks to dig into what went wrong before racing resumes.
key_points: Ferrari team principal **Fred Vasseur** admitted the team made "too many mistakes" during Sunday's Hungarian Grand Prix, a race its car was expected to suit.
Ferrari lost ground from the start: a poor getaway, a penalty, being **overtaken on track by Max Verstappen**, and repeated slow pit stops.
Both Ferrari drivers — **Charles Leclerc (4th) and Lewis Hamilton (5th)** — missed the podium despite the Hungaroring's layout suiting the car on paper.
Vasseur singled out pit-stop execution, saying the team lost positions over stops that were **0.2-0.3 seconds** slower than they should have been.
The admission comes just as F1 enters its **summer break**, giving Ferrari weeks to fix the issues before racing resumes.

depth.background: Formula 1 team principals are effectively CEOs of their racing operations, responsible for strategy calls, pit-stop execution, and managing driver dynamics — when a team underperforms, the principal is the one who fronts up to explain why. Ferrari came into the Hungarian Grand Prix weekend with genuine optimism: the Hungaroring's slow, twisty corners were expected to favour its car's strengths over faster circuits, making a result well below expectations sting more.

stories.title: Assam's flood death toll rises to 68, but the water is finally receding upcountry
stories.what_happened: Assam's flood death toll rose to 68 after two more deaths were reported from Charaideo district over the weekend, state officials said Monday. Charaideo remains the worst-affected district, with nearly 1.9 lakh people still under water there. Despite the higher toll, the overall number of people affected across the state actually fell from about 6.5 lakh to 5.24 lakh, as floodwaters recede in Upper Assam. Authorities are running 354 relief camps and distribution centres in four districts, currently sheltering more than 37,000 displaced people, and are now focusing on restoring electricity and other services as the water pulls back.
key_points: Death toll climbs to 68 after two more deaths in Charaideo district
But the number of affected people actually falls, from 6.5 lakh to 5.24 lakh
354 relief camps now sheltering more than 37,000 displaced people
Floodwaters receding in Upper Assam; focus shifting to relief and restoring power

depth.background: Assam sits on the Brahmaputra river system and floods almost every monsoon (June-September) as the river and its tributaries overflow. This year's flooding has been especially severe, submerging low-lying districts, destroying crops and homes, and forcing hundreds of thousands into relief camps.

thread.previously: As of Sunday, Assam's 2026 floods had killed 66 people and affected roughly 6.5 lakh (650,000) people, with Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal calling the situation 'extremely critical'.
thread.changed: The toll has risen to 68 after two more deaths in Charaideo district, but the number of people affected has actually fallen to about 5.24 lakh (524,000) as floodwaters recede across Upper Assam; the state's focus is shifting from rescue to relief and restoring power.

stories.title: Karnataka's reservoirs sink to their second-lowest level in 6 years as the CM warns of a severe drought
stories.what_happened: Karnataka's Water Resources Department data, as of July 24, shows the state's 14 major reservoirs collectively holding 419.35 tmcft against a total capacity of 895.69 tmcft — only about 40% full, and the second-lowest level in six years. Linganamakki, the state's largest reservoir, is storing 38.76 tmcft against its 151.75 tmcft capacity, nearly 10 tmcft below where it stood during the 2023 drought. The Ghataprabha reservoir holds 27.24 tmcft, sharply down from 46.35 tmcft on the same date last year, and the Tungabhadra reservoir has just 29.47 tmcft of its 105.79 tmcft capacity. Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar has publicly warned the state may face a severe drought this year and urged farmers not to count on reservoir water for irrigation.
key_points: Karnataka's **14 major reservoirs** held just **419.35 tmcft** of water as of July 24 — against a combined capacity of **895.69 tmcft**, or only **40% full**.
That's the state's **second-lowest reservoir level in 6 years**, driven by a weak monsoon.
The **Linganamakki** reservoir, Karnataka's largest, is even lower than during the **2023 drought year**.
The **Tungabhadra** reservoir is at just **29.47 tmcft** against a capacity of **105.79 tmcft**.
CM **D.K. Shivakumar** has warned of a potentially severe drought and urged farmers not to rely on reservoir water for their crops.

depth.background: Karnataka depends heavily on its network of major reservoirs — fed by monsoon rains — for drinking water, irrigation, and hydropower. This comes just after Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar traveled to Delhi with the state's full contingent of MPs to jointly lobby the central government for drought-relief funds. **Tmcft** ('thousand million cubic feet') is the standard unit India uses to measure reservoir storage.

thread.previously: Karnataka's Chief Minister summoned every state MP to Delhi to make a united, cross-party case to the central government for drought-relief funding.
thread.changed: Fresh Water Resources Department data shows just how severe the shortfall is: reservoirs are at their second-lowest level in six years, only 40% full.

stories.title: Israel's West Bank crackdown widens to 300+ raided sites as Palestinians say they're nearing 'breaking point'
stories.what_happened: Israeli troops have spent the weekend and into Monday sweeping the West Bank: raiding more than **300 locations**, searching for what the military calls Hamas affiliates, arms traffickers and other suspected militants. In Tal itself, soldiers raided about 70 homes and detained roughly 50 people, sealing the house of the Palestinian involved in Friday's shooting. Detentions have spread well beyond Tal — to Jenin, Tubas, the Al-Far'a refugee camp, Ramallah, Al-Bireh and Hebron — with more than 70 people held in total. Troops also raided a hospital in Nablus as part of the operation. Alongside the military sweep, Jewish settlers have grown more aggressive, marauding through villages, spray-painting graffiti, and attempting to set two mosques on fire. By Monday, Palestinian residents were telling reporters the pressure from both settlers and soldiers was pushing the area toward a 'breaking point.'
key_points: Israeli forces have searched **more than 300 locations** across the West Bank since Friday's deadly clash.
The trigger: a shootout near the village of Tal killed **four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers** on July 24.
Over **70 Palestinians** have been detained, with troops raiding roughly **70 homes** in Tal alone.
The UN says **68 Palestinians** have been killed in the West Bank in 2026 so far, at least 13 by settlers.
Settlers have grown bolder alongside the military operation, attempting to **torch two mosques**.

depth.background: The West Bank is Palestinian territory that Israel has militarily occupied since 1967; roughly 500,000 Israeli settlers now live there alongside about 3 million Palestinians, and settler-Palestinian friction has been rising for years. On July 24, a confrontation broke out near the village of Tal, southwest of Nablus, after settlers raided the town — a Palestinian grabbed a security officer's weapon and a shootout followed, leaving **four Palestinians (from one family) and two Israeli soldiers dead**. Prime Minister **Netanyahu ordered a 'wide-scale military operation'** in response, which has intensified daily since.

stories.title: Lewis Hamilton admits he's "left too many points on the table" after a rough first season with Ferrari
stories.what_happened: Speaking after the Hungarian Grand Prix, Hamilton candidly assessed his recent form, saying the last few races have been costly and that he's left too many points on the table. He added that he doesn't yet have a clear mindset heading into next year, reflecting the toll of a difficult debut season with Ferrari. He noted he's still second in the drivers' championship with plenty of the season left, and separately pushed back on suggestions he's lost his love for racing despite the frustrations.
key_points: Hamilton said his recent races have been costly, admitting he's **"left too many points on the table"**
He said he **"doesn't have a mindset into next year"** yet, reflecting a difficult first Ferrari season
Despite the frustration, he's still **second in the championship**, with "a long way to go" left in the season
The comments come right after the Hungarian Grand Prix, as F1 heads into its summer break
Hamilton has separately said he still **"loves racing"** despite the struggles

depth.background: Lewis Hamilton, a seven-time world champion, made a high-profile switch from Mercedes to Ferrari for this season — one of the biggest driver moves in modern F1 history, given Ferrari's status as the sport's most storied team and Hamilton's decade-plus rivalry with it. The move was billed as a shot at an eighth title with a fresh team, but his first season in red has been bumpier than expected, including recent penalties and inconsistent race pace, fuelling speculation about his mindset and long-term fit at Ferrari.

stories.title: Opposition forces a showdown in Parliament over the July 20 police crackdown on NEET protesters
stories.what_happened: A week after the July 20 crackdown, opposition MPs used the first days back in Parliament to demand accountability for how it was handled. In the Lok Sabha, Congress MPs K.C. Venugopal, Manickam Tagore, Hibi Eden and Vijayakumar (Vijay Vasanth) each filed separate adjournment motions — a procedure used to interrupt the normal agenda for an urgent discussion — describing the police response as **'brutal, unprovoked, and disproportionate.'** DMK MP T.R. Baalu went further, seeking a discussion on banning the NEET exam altogether and an inquiry into the alleged use of 'lethal weapons' against students at Jantar Mantar. In the Rajya Sabha, Congress MPs Randeep Singh Surjewala, Renuka Chowdhury and Syed Naseer Hussain invoked **Rule 267** — which lets members ask for the day's business to be set aside — to force the same debate. The government has not yet agreed to the discussion; instead it has pushed ahead with introducing a new anti-paper-leak bill in the Lok Sabha as its answer to the wider controversy.
key_points: Congress MPs filed **adjournment motions** in the Lok Sabha over police action on **July 20**.
Rajya Sabha MPs invoked **Rule 267** to demand Question Hour be suspended for a debate.
Opposition calls the Delhi Police and **Rapid Action Force** response 'brutal' and 'disproportionate.'
The protest, dubbed **'Chalo Sansad,'** was over the **NEET-UG 2026 paper leak** and CBSE marking irregularities.
DMK's T.R. Baalu also sought a discussion on **banning NEET** entirely.

depth.background: On July 20, as Parliament's monsoon session opened, thousands of students, parents and protesters marched toward Parliament Street in a demonstration called 'Chalo Sansad' ('let's go to Parliament'). They were demanding accountability over the **2026 NEET-UG paper leak** and irregularities in CBSE's on-screen marking process — scandals that already forced the previous Education Minister's resignation. When protesters pushed against police barricades near Parliament, the **Delhi Police** and the **Rapid Action Force** responded with tear gas and lathi-charges (baton charges) at multiple locations, injuring several people. That crackdown has since become its own political flashpoint, separate from the original exam scandal.

stories.title: A grabbed steering wheel sends an MSRTC bus crashing into two parked school buses in Maharashtra
stories.what_happened: An MSRTC bus belonging to the Nilanga depot was travelling from Latur to Ausa on Monday afternoon when, around 1:30pm, it crashed into two school buses parked near a school in the Peth area. Eyewitnesses told police that a passenger suddenly moved up behind the driver's seat and grabbed the steering wheel, causing the driver to lose control. The bus veered off the road and struck the two parked school buses, which were waiting to pick up students but had no children aboard at the time. Several passengers on the MSRTC bus were injured and rushed to Vilasrao Deshmukh Government Medical College and Hospital in Latur. Police are still verifying the steering-wheel-grab account before confirming the exact cause. Witnesses praised the driver, saying he kept enough control to steer the bus roughly 100 feet into an open area after the initial impact, which they believe stopped the crash from involving even more vehicles.
key_points: An MSRTC (Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation) bus travelling from **Latur to Ausa** veered off the road and rammed two parked school buses around **1:30pm** on Monday.
Police are verifying eyewitness accounts that a passenger suddenly grabbed the steering wheel from behind the driver, causing him to lose control.
**Several passengers were injured** and taken to Vilasrao Deshmukh Government Medical College and Hospital in Latur.
The two school buses it hit were parked and empty at the time — no children were aboard them.
Witnesses say the driver's quick reaction — steering the bus nearly **100 feet** into open ground after the first impact — likely prevented a bigger pile-up.

depth.background: MSRTC is Maharashtra's state-run bus operator, running thousands of routes across the state including many rural stretches like the Latur-Ausa road in the Marathwada region. Bus safety has been a recurring concern in Maharashtra, with several fatal MSRTC crashes in recent years blamed on a mix of ageing vehicles, driver fatigue, and rash driving on rural highways.

stories.title: Wildfires force over 360,000 to flee France and Spain as Macron calls an emergency meeting
stories.what_happened: Wildfires that started in France's Gironde region last Wednesday have now forced more than **360,000 people** to evacuate their homes across France and Spain — one of the largest evacuations in French history. The fire has burned nearly **104,000 acres** in southwestern France and around **190,000 acres** in the Avila and Toledo areas west of Madrid. France has mobilized **2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel, and roughly 1,200 police officers** to contain the blazes. French President **Emmanuel Macron** is holding a crisis cabinet meeting today, while Spanish Prime Minister **Pedro Sánchez** is visiting fire-hit areas in Valencia. Forecasters warn a fresh heatwave pushing temperatures to **40°C (104°F)** or higher is due to arrive this week, which could further complicate firefighting efforts.
key_points: More than **360,000 people** have now been evacuated across France and Spain combined.
The fire started in France's **Gironde region** last Wednesday before spreading into Spain.
It has burned roughly **104,000 acres in France** and **190,000 acres** around Avila and Toledo in Spain.
France has deployed **2,500 firefighters, 1,500 soldiers, and 1,200 police** to fight the blazes.
A **new heatwave** with temperatures near **40°C (104°F)** is forecast to hit the region this week.

depth.background: Southwestern Europe has been battling an unusually severe wildfire season this July, driven by a prolonged heatwave and tinder-dry vegetation after weeks of little rain. The fires began in France's Gironde wine region — the same area hit by major fires in 2022 — before winds pushed the blaze across the border into Spain's Castile and León and Madrid regions. Spain's death toll from this month's fires already stood at **14**, with **10 people still missing**, before this latest evacuation surge. Emergency services across both countries have been stretched thin fighting fires simultaneously on multiple fronts.

thread.previously: We reported Spain's wildfire death toll had climbed to 14 for the month, with 10 people still missing, as fires burned across the country.
thread.changed: The evacuation count has surged past **360,000 people** across France and Spain combined — one of the largest evacuations in French history — and French President Emmanuel Macron has called a crisis cabinet meeting today as a fresh heatwave threatens to make things worse.

stories.title: F1 confirms Malaysia will host this year's Bahrain Grand Prix, as Middle East tensions keep reshaping the calendar
stories.what_happened: Formula 1 and the FIA confirmed that the actual Bahrain Grand Prix — not Qatar or Abu Dhabi — will be relocated this year, moving from Bahrain to Sepang, Malaysia, and taking place October 2-4. The event keeps its original name and sponsor (the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix) despite the change of country, and slots in between the Azerbaijan and Singapore races. The move still needs formal approval from the FIA's World Motor Sport Council.
key_points: Sepang International Circuit will host the 'Bahrain Grand Prix' on October 2-4
It's a straight relocation — same race name, same sponsor, different country
Malaysia last hosted F1 in 2017, when its own Grand Prix was dropped from the calendar
Still needs final sign-off from the FIA's World Motor Sport Council

depth.background: F1 had already been scrambling to protect races in the Gulf region as the wider Israel-Iran-linked conflict raised safety and logistics concerns; Qatar and Abu Dhabi's season-ending races were flagged as at risk, with Imola and Sepang lined up as contingency venues. Malaysia hosted a full Malaysian Grand Prix at Sepang from 1999 to 2017 before falling off the calendar over hosting costs.

stories.title: Carlos Sainz's Williams future stays in doubt as Audi's Bortoleto rules out a seat swap
stories.what_happened: Sainz confirmed he's asked his management team to keep him out of driver-market discussions for now, saying he'll use the summer break to calmly assess his options with his Williams contract still unresolved. Multiple reports say he's eyeing a possible move to Audi for 2027 — the same team he turned down two years ago — but Audi driver Gabriel Bortoleto said he is signed to the team "for many years," which reduces the seat availability Sainz might have been counting on. Separately, Kimi Antonelli heads into the break leading the drivers' championship by 50 points over Hamilton, having become the youngest driver to win at Monaco and the youngest to lead the championship in F1 history.
key_points: Carlos Sainz says he's asked his management to **keep him out of driver-market talk** while he decides his future over the summer break
Sainz has been linked to a move to **Audi** for 2027 — a team he **turned down two years ago** to join Williams instead
Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto says he's **signed "for many years"** at the team, closing off that potential escape route for Sainz
The uncertainty adds Sainz to a long list of drivers, including reigning leader **Kimi Antonelli**, navigating contract questions this summer
Antonelli heads into the break leading the championship by **50 points** over Hamilton, the biggest gap of his rookie-record title run

depth.background: Carlos Sainz left Ferrari after the 2024 season and joined Williams for 2025, a team on a long rebuild after years outside the sport's front-runners. That decision came after Sainz reportedly had — and passed on — interest from Audi, which is entering F1 fully as a works team starting in 2026 with backing from the Volkswagen Group. With Williams' progress and Sainz's own results under scrutiny, speculation has persisted that he could look to jump to a better-resourced team like Audi once his contract situation allows.

stories.title: Sir Garfield Sobers lies in state at Barbados's Parliament as the island prepares to bid its cricket legend farewell
stories.what_happened: Sobers' body is lying in state today in the Chamber of the House of Assembly at Barbados's Parliament Buildings in Bridgetown, open to members of the public from 7am to 2pm to pay their respects. Tonight, "From the Crease" — an evening of stories and tributes from cricket legends celebrating his life — takes place at Cricket Legends of Barbados starting at 6pm. Tomorrow his body will lie in state again, this time at Kensington Oval, before Wednesday's full state funeral and national thanksgiving service at the same ground, followed by a private burial at Coral Ridge Memorial Gardens.
key_points: Sobers' body is lying in state at Barbados's **Parliament Buildings** in Bridgetown today, open to the public from **7am to 2pm**
A tribute evening, **"From the Crease,"** with stories from cricket legends about Sobers' life, follows tonight at **6pm**
His body moves to **Kensington Oval** — the island's most famous cricket ground — tomorrow for further public tribute
The full **state funeral** is set for **Wednesday, July 29, at 10am** at Kensington Oval
Sobers, widely considered one of the greatest all-rounders in cricket history, died last Friday at **89**

depth.background: Sir Garfield Sobers is a national hero in Barbados and one of the most celebrated cricketers of all time, famous for his all-round ability with bat, ball, and in the field during a career that helped define West Indies cricket's golden era. He died last Friday at age 89, prompting Barbados's government to declare a National Day of Mourning and plan a full state funeral befitting his stature. Barbados's Prime Minister Mia Mottley has led the tribute planning, with events designed to let both the public at home and the cricketing diaspora abroad pay their respects.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Barbados was finalizing a full state funeral for Sobers on Wednesday, July 29 at Kensington Oval, with his body set to lie in state at Parliament on July 27 and then Kensington Oval on July 28, free tickets being distributed to gauge crowds, and PM Mia Mottley declaring a National Day of Mourning.
thread.changed: The lying-in-state at Parliament is now underway today (7am–2pm), alongside a newly-detailed tribute evening, "From the Crease," tonight at 6pm featuring cricket legends sharing stories about Sobers ahead of Wednesday's funeral.

stories.title: A Chinese memory-chip maker's stock soars 466% on its first day of trading, becoming China's most valuable listed company
stories.what_happened: CXMT listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange on Monday after raising **57.9 billion yuan (~$8.6 billion)** in the largest semiconductor IPO in mainland Chinese history. The stock opened well above its 8.66-yuan offer price and closed the session **up 466%** at 49 yuan, a move so sharp it generated **141 billion yuan in trading volume** — more than any single-day turnover ever recorded for an A-share stock. That surge lifted CXMT's market capitalization to roughly **$488 billion**, instantly making it more valuable than ICBC, one of the world's biggest banks, and China's most valuable domestically-listed company. Retail demand for the shares was oversubscribed by **212 times**, and because only a small sliver of shares was released for trading, even modest buying pushed the price up dramatically.
key_points: CXMT's shares closed **up 466%** on their Shanghai debut, rocketing from an IPO price of 8.66 yuan to 49 yuan
The IPO raised **57.9 billion yuan (about $8.6 billion)** — the largest semiconductor share sale ever on mainland China
The surge gave CXMT a **$488 billion market value**, overtaking Industrial and Commercial Bank of China as the country's most valuable onshore stock
CXMT makes **DRAM memory chips** — the same class of chip used in phones, laptops, and AI servers — and holds roughly **7.7% of the global DRAM market**
Retail investors oversubscribed the offering **212 times over**; only about 6.7% of shares were even tradable at listing

depth.background: CXMT, formally ChangXin Memory Technologies, is based in Hefei and is China's leading maker of DRAM — the fast, short-term memory chip that every computer, phone, and AI server needs to function, as distinct from the flash storage that holds files long-term. For years the global DRAM market has been dominated by just three companies: South Korea's **Samsung and SK Hynix**, and US-based **Micron**. Washington's export controls have cut off Chinese firms from the most advanced Western chipmaking tools, pushing Beijing to pour state and private capital into building a homegrown chip supply chain instead of depending on companies it can't fully trust or access.

stories.title: Oil prices sink nearly 7% as the US-Iran ceasefire holds and Tehran opens Strait of Hormuz talks
stories.what_happened: Crude oil futures dropped sharply on Monday as the ceasefire between the US and Iran continued to hold and Tehran reportedly opened talks with Oman over safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. **Brent crude for September delivery fell 7.3% to roughly $89.73 a barrel**, while **US WTI crude fell 6.5% to about $83.47**. The move reverses a big chunk of this month's spike, which had been driven by fears that fighting could spread and choke off the Strait or the Red Sea route Saudi Arabia increasingly uses to move crude. Global stock markets rose on the relief, even as US chip stocks separately sold off for unrelated reasons.
key_points: **Brent crude fell 7.3%** to around **$89.73 a barrel**; **US WTI crude dropped 6.5%** to about **$83.47**.
The trigger is a holding pause in US-Iran hostilities, with Tehran now talking to Oman about the **Strait of Hormuz**.
Oil had surged **almost 40% this month** as fighting spread from the Strait of Hormuz toward the Red Sea shipping route.
World stock markets broadly **rose** on the news, even as some individual sectors (like chips) sold off separately.

depth.background: Earlier in July, the US carried out two weeks of nightly airstrikes on Iran before halting them; Iran responded in kind, and the ceasefire has held into this week. Oil markets had been pricing in serious disruption risk because Iran sits on the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow waterway that roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through daily — any Iranian move to block or mine it would choke off a huge share of global supply. That fear, plus fighting that spilled into Red Sea shipping lanes, drove crude up nearly 40% this month.

stories.title: IDFC First Bank shares jump nearly 10% to a 52-week high after profit crosses ₹1,000 crore for the first time
stories.what_happened: IDFC First Bank's shares jumped as much as 9-10% on Monday to touch a 52-week high on the National Stock Exchange, a day after the bank reported its strongest-ever quarterly results. The stock opened at ₹86.30, up from Friday's close of ₹80.79, and touched an intraday high of ₹88.76; by 12:15pm IST it was trading around ₹85.47. The rally followed news that the bank's standalone net profit for the April-June quarter more than doubled year-on-year to **₹1,075 crore**, up 132.4% from ₹463 crore in the same quarter last year — the first time its quarterly profit has crossed the ₹1,000 crore mark. Net interest income (the gap between what a bank earns on loans and pays on deposits) rose 21% to ₹5,974 crore, while its gross bad-loan ratio improved to 1.51% from 1.97% a year earlier. Total customer business — loans plus deposits — grew 18.6% year-on-year to over ₹6 lakh crore. Several brokerages raised their price targets on the stock after the results.
key_points: IDFC First Bank's stock surged as much as **9-10%** Monday to a 52-week high, after posting its best-ever quarterly profit.
Net profit for the April-June quarter (Q1 FY27) more than doubled to **₹1,075 crore**, up **132%** from ₹463 crore a year earlier — crossing ₹1,000 crore for the first time in the bank's history.
**Bad loans improved**: gross NPA (loans borrowers have stopped repaying) fell to **1.51%** from 1.97% a year ago.
Total loans plus deposits grew **18.6%** year-on-year to over **₹6 lakh crore**.
Brokerages raised their price targets on the stock following the results, fuelling the rally.

depth.background: IDFC First Bank was formed in 2018 from the merger of infrastructure lender IDFC Bank and microfinance-focused Capital First, and has spent recent years building up its retail banking business — deposits and personal loans — after inheriting a legacy of stressed infrastructure loans. Indian banks report earnings every quarter, and a bank's net profit, loan growth, and bad-loan ratio are the numbers investors watch most closely to judge how healthy its lending book is.

stories.title: Punjab's AAP government faces its own paper-leak firestorm, days after Delhi's cost a minister his job
stories.what_happened: Delhi minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa (BJP) and Punjab Congress president Amarinder Singh Raja Warring have both publicly demanded the resignation of Punjab Education Minister Harjot Singh Bains, pointing to an alleged leak of a pharmacy officer recruitment exam paper that reportedly affected around 7,000 candidates after being sold for 'lakhs of rupees.' They also cited earlier alleged leaks under the AAP government — a 2022 Class 12 English exam and a 2025 PSSSB recruitment exam — arguing this is a pattern, not a one-off.
key_points: BJP and Congress both demand Punjab Education Minister Harjot Bains resign
Allegations center on a leaked pharmacy officer exam — around 7,000 students said to be affected
Comes right after Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan quit over the separate, national NEET leak
Opposition calls out AAP for 'double standards' — the party once demanded resignations over leaks itself

depth.background: India has been gripped for weeks by a national scandal over a leaked NEET exam — the medical college entrance test millions of students take — which forced Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign and triggered mass 'Chalo Sansad' protests in Delhi. Punjab is run by the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), the same party that governs Delhi and has long positioned itself as the anti-corruption, clean-governance alternative to the BJP and Congress.

stories.title: A fresh landslide shuts the Jammu-Srinagar highway, stranding 1,700 trucks and cutting off the Kashmir Valley's main road link
stories.what_happened: A landslide combined with shooting stones struck NH-44 near Dewal in Udhampur district early Monday morning, blocking the highway and leaving about 1,700 trucks and numerous passenger vehicles stranded between Udhampur and Banihal. The National Highway Authority of India deployed personnel and heavy machinery to clear the debris and repair the damaged stretch, prioritizing passenger vehicles on the single carriageway that remains usable while trucks continue to wait. Authorities separately closed the Pul Doda bridge after markings resembling cracks were spotted, a safety concern independent of the landslide itself. Officials suspended all fresh vehicular movement on the highway in both directions — from Jammu towards Srinagar, Doda, Ramban and Patnitop, and from Qazigund towards Jammu — until the road is inspected and declared safe. No casualties have been reported so far.
key_points: A landslide and falling rocks hit the **250-km Jammu-Srinagar National Highway (NH-44)** at Dewal in Udhampur district early Monday, blocking the Valley's only major road link.
Around **1,700 trucks** and numerous passenger vehicles were stranded between Udhampur and Banihal as debris covered the carriageway.
The **Pul Doda bridge** was separately closed after markings resembling cracks raised safety concerns.
The **National Highway Authority of India (NHAI)** deployed machinery to clear debris, prioritizing stranded passenger vehicles first.
Authorities suspended all fresh traffic in both directions until the highway is inspected and declared safe.

depth.background: The Jammu-Srinagar National Highway is the only major all-weather road connecting the Kashmir Valley to the rest of India, making it a lifeline for supplies, trade, and travel since rail and flight options are more limited and weather-dependent. The route runs through steep, geologically unstable Himalayan terrain that is prone to landslides every monsoon season, roughly June to September, when heavy rain loosens hillside slopes above the road. Closures like this one are common during the monsoon but can strand thousands of vehicles for days depending on how quickly debris can be cleared, and this closure adds to a season already marked by flooding and heavy rain across North India.

stories.title: RBI set to hold rates at 5.25% through 2026 even as inflation creeps above target
stories.what_happened: A Reuters poll conducted July 21-27 among **72 economists** found that **68 of them (95%)** expect the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee to leave the repo rate unchanged at **5.25%** when it meets August 3-5, and to hold it there for the rest of 2026. This comes even though India's **consumer price inflation rose to 4.38% in June**, the first time it has crossed the RBI's 4% target since January 2025. Despite that uptick, Governor Sanjay Malhotra has pushed back on rate-hike speculation, saying it's too early to have that conversation, as the central bank instead watches for how the Middle East war and its knock-on effect on oil prices might hit the Indian economy. Separately, the government will run a **₹20,000 crore buyback of government bonds** through the RBI on July 28, part of its routine debt management.
key_points: A Reuters poll of **72 economists** found **68 (95%)** expect the RBI to hold its repo rate at **5.25%** on August 5.
India's **retail inflation hit 4.38% in June** — the first reading **above the RBI's 4% target** since January 2025.
RBI Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** called it 'premature' to even discuss raising rates.
The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets **August 3-5**; a **₹20,000 crore government bond buyback** is set for July 28.

depth.background: The **repo rate** is the interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends to commercial banks — it's the RBI's main lever for controlling inflation and growth. Raise it, and borrowing gets more expensive across the economy, cooling demand and prices; cut it, and the reverse happens. The RBI's mandate is to keep retail inflation near **4%**, with a tolerance band of 2-6%. Through most of 2025 and early 2026, inflation stayed comfortably under that target, giving the RBI room to focus on supporting growth rather than fighting prices.

stories.title: Taiwan's food safety regulator blames 'poor raw material management' for the carcinogen scandal that hit 13,000+ businesses
stories.what_happened: Taiwan's Food and Drug Administration (TFDA) released the findings of its independent investigation on Monday into what actually caused the contamination in seven tainted batches of Central Union's cooking oil. The investigation concluded the company failed to properly manage raw materials that carry a higher inherent risk of contamination, and that stricter controls were needed at every stage — sourcing, in-process inspection, and final testing — to catch a problem like this before it reaches consumers. The findings come after weeks of escalating fallout: Central Union was fined a record NT$165.2 million for not reporting the contamination fast enough, more than 13,000 downstream businesses were affected, and two consumer groups have now filed lawsuits, including claims tied to school cafeterias that could total NT$6 billion.
key_points: TFDA's independent probe found **high-risk raw materials weren't properly controlled** at Central Union Oil's plant
The carcinogen **benzo[a]pyrene** was found at **more than 4x Taiwan's legal limit** in the company's soybean oil
**1,300+ tonnes** of tainted oil had already reached **over 13,000 businesses**, including schools, before the recall
Central Union was already fined a record **NT$165.2 million (~US$5.2m)** for not reporting the contamination immediately
Consumer groups are now suing over the tainted oil, with claims involving schools estimated to reach **NT$6 billion**

depth.background: The scandal broke in late June 2026, when Central Union Oil Corp. voluntarily reported that a self-inspection had found the carcinogen benzo[a]pyrene (BaP) in one batch of its soybean salad oil — Taiwan's legal limit is 2 micrograms per kilogram, and the tainted batch tested at more than four times that. What started as one flagged batch grew over the following weeks into a nationwide recall as inspectors found more contaminated batches, eventually implicating 1,300+ tonnes of oil already distributed to food manufacturers, restaurants and schools across the island. The scandal has become a political flashpoint, with the opposition Kuomintang (KMT) organizing a Taipei rally on July 25 accusing the government of mishandling the response.

stories.title: Pakistan-administered Kashmir votes under heavy security after a summer of deadly protests
stories.what_happened: Pakistan-administered Kashmir opened voting Monday in the first of three staggered rounds of local legislative elections, held under heavy security after a summer marked by violence. Protests demanding electoral reform escalated into deadly clashes, and even conservative counts put the death toll since early June at close to **30 people**, including protesters and law enforcement personnel. As polls opened, a political worker died in a scuffle between rival party supporters in the Kotli district's Nakyal area, and internet blackouts and roadblocks have periodically cut off parts of the region ahead of the vote. At the center of the unrest are **12 of the assembly's seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees** who resettled in Pakistan proper after the 1947 partition — protesters argue those seats should instead go to people who actually live in AJK today. Roughly 3.8 million residents are registered to vote in this first round, which covers the Mirpur division's 13 constituencies.
key_points: Voting opened Monday in the first of **three rounds** of local elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir (AJK), under heavy security.
Nearly **30 people have been killed** since June in protests and clashes over the vote — even before polling day.
The anger centers on **12 assembly seats** reserved for Kashmiri refugees who fled to Pakistan after **1947 Partition** but no longer live in the region.
A political worker died in scuffles between rival party supporters in Kotli district as voting got under way Monday.
About **3.8 million residents** are eligible to vote across the Pakistan-controlled part of the disputed Himalayan territory.

depth.background: Kashmir has been split and disputed between India and Pakistan since Partition in 1947, with Pakistan administering one slice — Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) — while India controls Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh; both countries claim the whole region, and China holds a smaller sliver. AJK holds its own local legislative elections roughly every five years, separate from Pakistan's national polls, to choose a government responsible for local administration while Islamabad keeps control of defence and foreign affairs. Long-simmering anger over how power and representation are shared — especially the seats reserved for Kashmiri refugee-descendants who no longer live in AJK — boiled into open protest this summer.

stories.title: The US-Iran strike pause holds into a new week as Tehran matches it with a halt of its own
stories.what_happened: For a fourth consecutive day, the Pentagon has not launched new strikes on Iran. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran will keep its own retaliatory attacks on hold as long as the US does the same, and Iran's army spokesman confirmed operations in the Gulf have stopped. US officials, including UN Ambassador Mike Waltz, say the quiet is intentional, meant to give ongoing talks room to progress.
key_points: No US strikes on Iran for a 4th straight day
Iran's army says it has also halted retaliatory operations in the Gulf
Trump's advisers reportedly cited a dwindling target list and munitions concerns
US Ambassador Mike Waltz says the pause is meant to let talks 'develop'

depth.background: The US and Iran have effectively been at war since a 13-night US bombing campaign hit Iranian nuclear and military sites after the Hormuz shipping crisis escalated. That intensity dropped when Washington quietly paused strikes late last week.

thread.previously: The US quietly paused a two-week bombing campaign against Iran's nuclear and military sites, and extended that pause into a second day while a compromise on Hormuz shipping took shape.
thread.changed: Iran has now formally matched the US pause — a senior Iranian official said Tehran will hold its own retaliatory strikes as long as Washington does, and Iran's army said it halted operations in the Gulf. Trump's team says the quiet is deliberately giving talks 'space' to progress.

stories.title: Jasprit Bumrah's Sri Lanka Test spot slips further into doubt as India's squad picture firms up
stories.what_happened: India's selectors were set to meet virtually on Monday to finalize the Test squad for next month's Sri Lanka tour, with Jasprit Bumrah's fitness the biggest lingering question. Bumrah picked up a knee injury while fielding in the second ODI against England in Cardiff on **July 17**, and reactive swelling overnight forced him out of the third ODI two days later. Team management has advised him to rest completely until **July 30**, after which he'll travel to the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru for rehabilitation work and a final fitness scan before any decision on his availability. Multiple reports on Monday said Bumrah has not yet regained full fitness and is now considered unlikely to feature in the two-Test series. In contrast, all-rounder Ravindra Jadeja — who like Bumrah had been in the "fitness-watch" category — has been declared fit and is expected to return after recovering from a tennis-elbow injury picked up during IPL 2026. The first Test starts August 15 in Galle, with the second beginning August 23 in Colombo.
key_points: **Jasprit Bumrah**, India's No.1-ranked Test bowler, is now considered **unlikely to play** the Sri Lanka Tests as his left-knee injury clearance drags on.
Bumrah hurt his knee fielding in the **2nd ODI against England in Cardiff on July 17**; swelling forced him out of the 3rd ODI two days later.
The team management has told him to **rest completely until July 30**, then report to the BCCI's Centre of Excellence for a final fitness scan.
By contrast, **Ravindra Jadeja** — in the same fitness-watch bracket as Bumrah — has now been **cleared fit** and is set to return.
India's selectors were expected to meet Monday to finalize the squad; the two-Test series against Sri Lanka begins **August 15 in Galle**.

depth.background: Jasprit Bumrah is India's premier fast bowler and the ICC's top-ranked Test bowler, but has battled recurring injury and workload issues over the past two years, with the team carefully managing how much he plays to protect his fitness for the biggest series. India's tour of Sri Lanka — two Tests starting August 15 in Galle — is part of the ongoing 2025-27 World Test Championship cycle, making squad selection especially high-stakes for India's qualification hopes for the WTC final.

thread.previously: Yesterday's reports had Bumrah included in India's squad for the Sri Lanka Tests but flagged as 'fitness-watched' — his spot conditional on clearing a fitness test after a knee issue.
thread.changed: Today, multiple reports say Bumrah still hasn't regained full fitness and is now considered unlikely to play any part of the Sri Lanka series, while Jadeja — in the same fitness-watch bracket yesterday — has been cleared fit and is set to return.

stories.title: A petrol bomb is hurled at a BJP office in Punjab's Sangrur overnight
stories.what_happened: Late Sunday night or in the early hours of Monday, someone threw a petrol bomb — a bottle filled with fuel and set alight — over the garden wall of the BJP's office in Sangrur, Punjab. It landed between two sections of the building, leaving visible fire damage, but caused no reported injuries. Police were alerted Monday morning and are now reviewing CCTV footage from the area to identify who was responsible. Sangrur SP Devendra Atri confirmed the incident and said an investigation is underway.
key_points: A petrol bomb was thrown at the **BJP office in Sangrur, Punjab**, late Sunday night into Monday morning.
The bottle landed **between two sections** of the building after being thrown over a garden wall, with visible **signs of fire**.
**No injuries** have been reported; police are reviewing **CCTV footage** to identify the attackers.
Sangrur SP **Devendra Atri** confirmed police received the report Monday morning and are investigating.

depth.background: Sangrur is a district in Punjab, a state currently governed by the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), where the BJP sits in opposition. Attacks and vandalism at political party offices are not uncommon amid Punjab's often-heated politics, and this incident lands during a period of national political tension around the NEET exam paper-leak protests, plus Punjab's own recent paper-leak controversy involving an AAP minister.

stories.title: A shootout between two gunmen at Seattle's 'Bite of Seattle' festival kills 3, wounds 4 — including a toddler
stories.what_happened: Shortly before 6 p.m. on Sunday, gunfire broke out at the Bite of Seattle festival at Seattle Center, with police saying it appears two people were shooting at each other in the crowd. Officers working nearby rushed in and confronted one of the shooters, an intervention police say kept the toll from being worse; that suspect was taken into custody and two guns were recovered. Three people died — two pronounced dead at the scene despite CPR, and a 56-year-old woman who died later at Harborview Medical Center. Four more people were wounded, including a 2-year-old child, and were taken to hospital in stable condition. Police believe a second shooter was also involved and are actively searching for that person. The motive and relationship between the shooters has not yet been made public.
key_points: **Three people killed** and four wounded, including a **2-year-old**, when gunfire erupted at the Bite of Seattle food festival
Police believe **two shooters were firing at each other** in a crowd near Seattle Center and the Space Needle
Officers **confronted one shooter directly**, which police credit with preventing more casualties; a **second suspect is still at large**
The gunfire broke out around **6 p.m. Sunday**, and **two guns** were recovered at the scene
A 56-year-old woman died later at **Harborview Medical Center**; three other victims, including the toddler, are in stable condition

depth.background: Seattle Center is a large public park and festival ground next to the Space Needle, and it regularly hosts family-friendly summer events — Bite of Seattle is one of the city's biggest, drawing tens of thousands of people over a weekend to sample food from dozens of local restaurants. Gun violence at large US public gatherings has become a recurring story in recent years, from concerts to parades to festivals, regardless of a city's overall crime rate. Seattle police say they already had officers working in the area for festival security, which is part of why the response was fast.

stories.title: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat says LGBTQ+ people 'have a right to live' in society, while calling live-in relationships a 'blind imitation' of the West
stories.what_happened: Speaking at an event on contemporary motherhood in Hyderabad, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat said LGBTQ+ people are part of society, deserve dignity, and should not be isolated, adding that some sexual orientations are innate ('determined by nature itself') while others may be shaped by upbringing or circumstance, and that Indian tradition had long quietly made space for such communities. In the same address, he described marriage as instilling discipline and responsibility, called live-in relationships a 'blind imitation' of Western culture, said modernity was nonetheless necessary, and urged parents to limit mobile-phone use and talk more with their children.
key_points: Bhagwat: LGBTQ+ people are 'part of society' and deserve 'dignity and their own space'
He said Indian tradition had long recognised such communities quietly
Separately, he called marriage a discipline and live-in relationships a copy of Western culture
He also urged parents to practise 'mobile-phone discipline' and talk more with their children
Remarks came at an event on contemporary motherhood in Hyderabad
The RSS is the ideological parent organisation of India's ruling BJP

depth.background: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) is a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation and the ideological parent body of India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) — its chief's public remarks are widely read as signals of where the broader Hindu-nationalist movement, and sometimes the government, stands on social questions, even though the RSS itself holds no formal government role. India decriminalised gay sex in 2018, but the Supreme Court declined to legalise same-sex marriage in 2023, leaving LGBTQ+ rights a live and contested social debate.

stories.title: Sudan's Army Retakes Key Highway as El-Obeid Braces for a Possible Genocide-Level Siege
stories.what_happened: Sudan's army announced Sunday it had regained full control of the Al Sadarat highway, the main road linking Khartoum to El-Obeid, after driving out RSF fighters who had held it. The army said the operation inflicted heavy losses on RSF troops and forced them to retreat from towns along the route. Controlling the highway lets the army move troops, weapons, fuel and supplies into the besieged city and cuts off one of the RSF's main routes for pushing toward it. Even with the highway recaptured, El-Obeid remains encircled and under near-daily drone bombardment from both sides, striking markets, schools, water infrastructure and fuel stations. The UN's human rights chief, Volker Türk, has publicly warned that the city's civilians are being subjected to 'relentless' attacks as fears grow of a full RSF ground assault.
key_points: Sudan's army said it recaptured the **Al Sadarat highway** linking capital Khartoum to **El-Obeid** on Sunday, after two days of fierce fighting with the paramilitary **Rapid Support Forces (RSF)**.

El-Obeid, capital of North Kordofan state, has swelled to roughly **500,000** people as displaced Sudanese flee into it — and it remains besieged, with UN investigators warning it could become the next **El-Fasher**.

In just three weeks in June alone, the UN documented **15 drone strikes** on El-Obeid that killed at least **45 civilians**; drone strikes by both sides have killed over **1,000** people across the wider Kordofan region since January 2026.

A UN Fact-Finding Mission ruled on **July 9** that RSF's mass killings, gang rape and deliberate starvation during its 18-month siege of El-Fasher amounted to **genocide** against the non-Arab Zaghawa and Fur communities.
Food prices in besieged El-Obeid have surged by as much as **300%**, and residents say they can no longer afford to eat or to flee the city.

depth.background: Sudan has been at war since **April 2023**, when the regular army (SAF) split violently from its former partner, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in a struggle for control of the country. The war has displaced more people than any other conflict on Earth and left around **5 million** Sudanese facing emergency or catastrophic hunger. Earlier this year the RSF captured El-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, after an 18-month siege marked by mass killings later ruled to be genocide by UN investigators — a precedent that has raised alarm that El-Obeid, Kordofan's regional capital, could suffer the same fate.

stories.title: Verstappen brands Racing Bulls drivers 'morons' after blue-flag system failure costs him time
stories.what_happened: Mid-race, Verstappen caught up to lap Lawson and Lindblad, who were battling each other for their own position and went side-by-side into a corner instead of immediately yielding. That cost Verstappen time as he pushed for a strong finish. He erupted over team radio, demanding the pair be penalized and calling them 'morons.' It later emerged the blue-flag light-panel system in the cars had malfunctioned, so race control had to revert to manual marshalling with flags — meaning several drivers, including Lawson and Lindblad, may not have clearly seen the signal telling them to move over. Given the technical failure, stewards issued no penalty to either Racing Bulls driver. Verstappen crossed the line second behind Norris, while Lawson finished eighth and Lindblad tenth, both inside the points.
key_points: Verstappen ripped into Racing Bulls pair **Liam Lawson** and **Arvid Lindblad** on untelevised radio, calling them **'morons'** for not yielding while he tried to lap them
Cause: a **light-panel system failure** meant blue flags weren't showing properly in cockpits, forcing marshals to fall back on manual flag-waving
His exact radio quote: *"Oh, they should get a penalty. This is f***ing ridiculous, these morons! My God"*
Verstappen still finished **P2**, 15 seconds behind winner Lando Norris, so the delay didn't cost him the podium
**Race control took no action** against either Racing Bulls driver once the system fault came to light; Lawson (P8) and Lindblad (P10) both scored points

depth.background: A blue flag (shown on track and as a light on the steering wheel) tells a lapped, slower car to immediately let a faster leader through. Racing Bulls is Red Bull's junior sister team, developing young talent like rookie Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson, but the two squads race as full rivals on track. Verstappen, Red Bull's four-time champion, is fighting to close ground in a title race Mercedes rookie Kimi Antonelli currently leads.

stories.title: DR Congo's Ebola outbreak tops 3,000 cases, spreading faster than any Ebola outbreak on record
stories.what_happened: The Democratic Republic of Congo's health ministry has now confirmed more than **3,075 Ebola cases and 1,354 deaths** since the outbreak began, spread across five provinces including Ituri (the hardest-hit, with roughly 90% of cases) and North Kivu. Case numbers have accelerated sharply, adding about 1,000 new confirmed cases in just the ten days before July 27 — a pace doctors say outstrips prior DRC outbreaks. In mid-July, a crowd angered by a hospital death stormed the **Nyakunde hospital** in Ituri province, forcing Ebola patients and responding medical staff — including the aid group Samaritan's Purse — to flee, and some too-sick-to-move patients were left without treatment. The **UN peacekeeping mission (MONUSCO)** has since deployed a base near Nyakunde to help protect health workers going forward. The virus has also spread beyond DRC's borders: Uganda has confirmed 20 cases, and individual patients have been medically evacuated to Germany and France for treatment.
key_points: Confirmed cases have passed **3,075**, with **1,354 deaths**, across **five provinces** of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The outbreak hit **1,000 confirmed cases in just 40 days** — the 2018 North Kivu outbreak took **235 days** to reach the same mark.
Roughly **1,000 new cases were added in just the last 10 days**, prompting doctors to describe it as spreading '**like wildfire**.'
An angry mob **attacked a hospital in Nyakunde**, forcing Ebola patients and medical staff to flee, disrupting the response in the worst-hit province.
The virus has already **crossed borders**, with imported cases confirmed in Uganda, and travelers evacuated to Germany and France for treatment.

depth.background: Ebola is a severe, often-fatal viral disease spread through contact with bodily fluids of infected people; the strain driving this outbreak is the **Bundibugyo virus**, one of several Ebola-family viruses. The Democratic Republic of Congo has dealt with Ebola outbreaks before — including the 2018-2020 North Kivu outbreak, one of the worst in history — so the country has real experience and infrastructure for fighting it. This is the DRC's **17th recorded Ebola outbreak**, but responders say it is moving unusually fast: security problems in the eastern provinces, where armed groups operate and distrust of health workers runs high, have repeatedly disrupted containment efforts, including attacks on treatment centers and burial teams.

stories.title: Deportation protections for 300,000+ Haitians in the US expire today, and ICE is ready to move
stories.what_happened: The US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit's temporary block on revoking Haitian TPS status expires today, after the court pushed the deadline back multiple times since late June while weighing the government's case. Unless a last-minute order intervenes, roughly **300,000 Haitians** living legally in the US under TPS lose that protection and their work permits starting today. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been preparing targeted operations to arrest and deport Haitian migrants, according to internal documents reported by CBS News, with Ohio — home to a large Haitian population in cities like Springfield — identified as an early target. The Supreme Court already cleared the way for this on **June 25**, in a ruling that also stripped protections from about 6,000 Syrians, so today's expiry is procedural rather than a new legal decision. Affected migrants can accept a government-funded flight and a $2,600 payment to leave voluntarily, or risk arrest and forced deportation. An estimated 145,000 of the affected Haitians live in Florida alone, including roughly 36,000 in health care roles.
key_points: A federal appeals court's temporary block on ending **Temporary Protected Status (TPS)** for Haitians expires **today, July 27**, clearing the way to strip protections from roughly **300,000 Haitians**.
ICE has been preparing targeted enforcement operations, including in **Ohio**, home to a large Haitian community, with deportation flights reportedly able to begin within days.
The **US Supreme Court** already ruled on **June 25** that the administration could proceed with ending TPS for Haiti and Syria, so today's deadline is the last of three court-ordered delays.
Roughly **145,000** of the affected Haitians live in Florida, including about **36,000** working in health care.
Migrants who leave voluntarily can be offered a government-funded flight home plus a **$2,600** payment.

depth.background: Temporary Protected Status lets people from countries hit by war, disaster, or crisis live and work in the US legally, without a path to citizenship, as long as their home country's designation stays active. Haiti has held TPS for over a decade because of gang violence, political collapse, and a 2021 earthquake that made large parts of the country unsafe to return to. The administration moved to end Haiti's TPS status earlier this year, arguing conditions no longer justify it — a decision challenged in court as endangering people who fled genuine danger. The Supreme Court sided with the administration on **June 25**, but a federal appeals court kept issuing short extensions, pushing the deadline back three times, with today marking the final one's expiry.

stories.title: Houthi drones strike Saudi Arabia's main east-west oil pipeline, widening the Yemen war's reach into the kingdom's oil backbone
stories.what_happened: On Monday, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched drone strikes on facilities along Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline, known as Petroline, which moves oil roughly 1,200 km from the kingdom's eastern fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. The pipeline normally runs at its full capacity of **7 million barrels a day** and exists partly so Saudi Arabia can export oil without routing tankers through the Strait of Hormuz. Saree said the attack targeted supply and transport points, framing it as retaliation for repeated Saudi drone flights over Yemeni territory. Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Defense confirmed its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several drones, with no reported casualties or disruption to pipeline flows. This is the third major Houthi strike on Saudi oil infrastructure within a week, after attacks on Aramco's Jizan and Yanbu refineries on July 25 briefly pushed Brent crude above $100 a barrel. Shipping through the nearby Bab el-Mandeb Strait has already fallen to its lowest level in months as vessels avoid the area.
key_points: Yemen's Houthi rebels launched drone strikes today targeting Saudi Arabia's **Petroline**, the pipeline that carries **7 million barrels a day** from eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the strikes hit pumping and transport points, calling it retaliation for **repeated Saudi drone incursions into Yemeni airspace**.
Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Defense said its air defenses **intercepted and destroyed** the attacking drones before any damage.
It follows Houthi strikes on Aramco refineries in **Jizan and Yanbu** days earlier that sent Brent crude above **$100 a barrel**.
The Houthis have also declared a **naval blockade** of Saudi ports this month, marking a sharp escalation from the years-long truce.

depth.background: Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement held an uneasy truce for several years after a brutal civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis seized Yemen's capital Sanaa and a Saudi-led coalition intervened to back the internationally recognized government. That truce unraveled this month after a Saudi strike on Sanaa's airport aimed at stopping an Iranian plane from landing, provoking the Houthis into firing missiles at Saudi Arabia and declaring a **blockade** of its ports. The Houthis are part of Iran's regional network of allied armed groups, and their return to open conflict has opened a new front in the wider **US-Israel-Iran confrontation** that has dominated the region this year. Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure was last hit at this scale roughly four years ago.

thread.previously: Houthi strikes on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea sent Brent crude above $100 a barrel for the first time since May, before prices eased back to around $97-98 by July 24.
thread.changed: The Houthis have now struck Saudi Arabia's main East-West pipeline directly rather than tankers at sea — hitting fixed oil infrastructure inside Saudi territory, though Saudi air defenses say they intercepted the drones this time.

stories.title: Nvidia stock jumps as its $500 billion South Korea chip deal starts paying off
stories.what_happened: SK Group -- South Korea's second-largest conglomerate -- and Nvidia announced a partnership worth more than $500 billion covering both new AI data centers and a long-term memory-chip supply deal. SK Telecom will build a 2-gigawatt AI computing facility using Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin chip platform, running on advanced HBM4 memory made by SK Hynix, with the first facility due online in 2027. On Monday, Nvidia's stock jumped more than 3% as investors reacted positively, even though SK Hynix's own share price stayed largely flat.
key_points: Nvidia and SK Group struck a partnership worth $500+ billion for AI infrastructure
SK Telecom will build a 2-gigawatt AI data center using Nvidia's next-gen chips
SK Hynix is locked in as Nvidia's long-term AI memory-chip supplier
Nvidia shares jumped over 3% Monday; SK Hynix's own stock barely moved

depth.background: Nvidia's AI chips are only as fast as the memory feeding them data, and the world depends on a small number of Asian chipmakers -- mainly SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron -- for that memory. Building AI 'factories' (giant data centers packed with chips) also needs huge amounts of electricity and construction, which is why Nvidia increasingly partners directly with power and telecom companies instead of just selling chips to them.

stories.title: China's industrial profit growth slows to its weakest pace this year
stories.what_happened: Data released Monday by China's National Bureau of Statistics showed industrial profits rose 15.1% year-on-year in June, down from May's 21.1% gain - a second consecutive month of slowing growth as easing energy prices removed some of the tailwind behind this year's rebound. First-half profits are up 18.7%.
key_points: Industrial profits rose 15.1% year-on-year in June, down from 21.1% in May
Second straight month of deceleration as energy and oil prices ease
H1 2026 profits are still up 18.7%, a strong number but slightly down from Jan-May's 18.8%
An AI-driven boom in chip and equipment manufacturing had been a key growth driver this year

depth.background: China's industrial profits swung from barely-positive growth in 2025 to double-digit gains this year, helped by an AI-driven boom in chip and equipment manufacturing and the tail end of nearly three years of factory-gate deflation - falling wholesale prices that had been squeezing manufacturers' margins.

stories.title: Red Bull dangles an ownership stake to stop Verstappen walking to a rival
stories.what_happened: Multiple reports say Red Bull is trying to head off an exit by restructuring Verstappen's contract: extending it a further year to 2029, removing the exit clause entirely, raising his reported base salary (around €65m), and — most strikingly — potentially offering him an equity stake in the team itself, something no active F1 driver has ever held.
key_points: Red Bull reportedly open to extending Verstappen's deal by a year, to 2029
Talk of an equity stake that would make him the most powerful driver in F1 history
His current deal lets him leave if he's outside the top two in the standings at the summer break
Comes right after a shaky Hungarian GP where Red Bull admitted it hasn't built him a car to attack with

depth.background: Max Verstappen is a four-time world champion contracted to Red Bull through 2028 — but with an unusual 'performance exit clause': a get-out that lets him leave early if the team isn't delivering, tied to where he stands in the championship at the summer break. Red Bull's car has struggled to match the front-runners this season, which is exactly why that clause has become the story of the year, with rivals like Mercedes and McLaren circling.

stories.title: Honda's next-gen F1 engine gets its first real test — two years before it matters
stories.what_happened: Fresh off the Hungarian Grand Prix, where Aston Martin's new B-spec AMR26 car showed a clear step in pace, Honda will run an updated version of its power unit for the first time at a filming day at the Hungaroring this Wednesday. Reserve driver Jak Crawford will do the running, limited to 200km under filming-day rules. It's a shakedown ahead of the engine's official race debut at the Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort on August 21-23.
key_points: Honda will run its updated power unit at an Aston Martin filming day at the Hungaroring on Wednesday
Reserve driver Jak Crawford does the running, capped at 200km
It comes right after Aston Martin's B-spec car showed a clear pace jump at the Hungarian GP
The engine's official race debut is at Zandvoort, August 21-23

depth.background: Honda officially became Aston Martin's power-unit partner starting in 2026, ending its long Red Bull partnership. F1 rules cap pre-season and in-season track running tightly, so teams use 'filming days' — technically for promotional footage — to sneak in real engineering mileage on new parts.

stories.title: China's Moonshot AI releases the full weights of its Kimi K3 model today, sharpening the fight over 'open' AI
stories.what_happened: Moonshot AI says it is releasing Kimi K3's full model weights today, July 27 — the actual downloadable parameters, not just cloud access. That makes it far easier for developers and researchers everywhere, including in the US, to run and study the model directly on their own hardware. The release follows a chaotic two weeks in which demand for Kimi K3 overwhelmed Moonshot's computing capacity, forcing the company to briefly halt new subscriptions.
key_points: Moonshot AI is releasing Kimi K3's full downloadable parameters today, July 27
The 2.8-trillion-parameter model rivals GPT and Claude on many benchmarks — for free
Demand overwhelmed Moonshot's servers, forcing a brief subscription pause
US officials and Anthropic accuse Moonshot of 'distilling' American models; Moonshot denies it

depth.background: Kimi K3 first appeared in mid-July from Beijing-based Moonshot AI, a relatively unknown startup, and stunned the AI world by nearly matching the best US systems on many tests while being free to use. It's an 'open-weight' model, meaning anyone can download and run its underlying parameters rather than only accessing it through a paid API — the AI equivalent of open-sourcing the recipe, not just selling the finished dish. US officials, alarmed at how fast Chinese labs are closing the gap, have accused Moonshot of 'distillation' — training its model by learning from the outputs of American models like GPT and Claude, a shortcut that's controversial but hard to prove. Days ago, over 50 US tech and policy figures signed a letter urging Washington not to overreact and to keep supporting America's own open-weight AI efforts rather than simply trying to block China's.

thread.previously: We reported that over 50 US tech and policy figures signed a letter urging Washington to keep supporting America's own open-weight AI development rather than simply moving to block Chinese models, as the US weighed curbs on them.
thread.changed: The Chinese model at the center of that debate, Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, released its full downloadable weights today, escalating exactly the dynamic the letter warned about — a free, open Chinese alternative undercutting paid US AI products.

stories.title: Masood's gritty fifty leads Pakistan's fightback on Day 3 in Trinidad, but Babar falls late
stories.what_happened: Pakistan extended their reply through Day 3, built on a 155-run second-wicket partnership between Imam-ul-Haq and captain Shan Masood after Imam was caught at slip. Masood slowed down in the evening session to see out the day unbeaten on 88, but West Indies fast bowler Jayden Seales struck late to remove Babar Azam. Pakistan closed the day on 199/3, still trailing West Indies' 311 by 112 runs, with Salman Ali Agha new at the crease.
key_points: Pakistan closed Day 3 at 199/3, trailing West Indies' first-innings 311
Shan Masood unbeaten on 88, anchoring after a 155-run stand with Imam-ul-Haq
Babar Azam fell late to Jayden Seales after playing a supporting role
Salman Ali Agha is the new man in, yet to score

depth.background: We reported that West Indies were bowled out for 311 on Day 2 of this first Test in Tarouba, Trinidad, with Pakistan reaching 60/1 in reply at that day's stumps. The five-day match, part of Pakistan's tour of the West Indies, runs July 25-29.

thread.previously: We reported West Indies were bowled out for 311 on Day 2, with Pakistan reaching 60/1 in reply at stumps.
thread.changed: Pakistan extended their reply to 199/3 by the close of Day 3, built on a 155-run stand between Imam-ul-Haq and Shan Masood, before Babar Azam fell late.

stories.title: Sonam Wangchuk leaves hospital after his 26-day hunger strike, heads to Rajghat before returning to Ladakh
stories.what_happened: Wangchuk walked out of Medanta Hospital in Gurugram on Monday, July 27, days after his health seriously deteriorated during a **26-day hunger strike** that began June 28 at Jantar Mantar. He lost roughly 8 to 10 kg over the course of the fast. He ended the strike on July 24 after the central government agreed to accept all his demands relating to the paper-leak scandal, breaking his fast with juice offered by Union Health Minister JP Nadda at his bedside. Hospital officials said he is now on a liquid diet and in stable health. After discharge, Wangchuk said his first stop would be Rajghat to pay tribute to Mahatma Gandhi — mirroring a visit he made there just before starting the fast — before he heads home to Ladakh to resume his environmental and education work.
key_points: Climate activist **Sonam Wangchuk** was discharged from Gurugram's **Medanta Hospital** after ending a **26-day hunger strike**.
He lost an estimated **8 to 10 kg** during the fast, which he began at Jantar Mantar in support of students hit by the **NEET paper-leak scandal**.
He broke his fast on **July 24** after the central government agreed to **all his demands**, with Union Health Minister JP Nadda present to offer him juice.
His first stop after discharge is **Rajghat**, Mahatma Gandhi's memorial, before he returns home to **Ladakh**.
It echoes his own history: Wangchuk visited Rajghat before starting the fast too, and was previously **jailed for six months** in connection with earlier Ladakh statehood protests.

depth.background: Sonam Wangchuk is a well-known Indian engineer-turned-education-and-climate activist from Ladakh, famous for inventing low-cost solar-heated buildings and for inspiring the engineer character in the film *3 Idiots*. He has spent years campaigning for **Ladakh statehood and Sixth Schedule protection** (special constitutional safeguards for tribal areas), and was jailed for six months earlier in 2026 over related protests before his release in March. In late June he began a fresh hunger strike at Delhi's Jantar Mantar, this time over the **NEET exam paper-leak scandal** and alleged irregularities in CBSE's on-screen marking process, which had triggered nationwide student protests and a police crackdown that Parliament has been fighting over for days.

stories.title: IMD red alert: a deep depression is set to cross the Odisha-Bengal coast today, schools shut in three districts
stories.what_happened: IMD said a deep depression over the northwest Bay of Bengal, close to the West Bengal-north Odisha coast, is expected to move north-northwestwards and cross the coast between Balasore and Canning around the afternoon of July 27. A red alert for extremely heavy rainfall is in force, and schools are shut in Mayurbhanj, Jagatsinghpur and Kendrapara.
key_points: A deep depression over the northwest Bay of Bengal is set to cross the coast near Balasore and Canning this afternoon
IMD has issued a red alert - its highest warning level - for extremely heavy rainfall
Schools are shut in Mayurbhanj, Jagatsinghpur and Kendrapara districts
Fishermen have been told to stay off the sea until the system passes

depth.background: Odisha and coastal West Bengal sit in a monsoon-season corridor that regularly sees low-pressure systems form over the Bay of Bengal and cross the coast, bringing intense rain and flash-flood risk. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) grades these warnings green, yellow, orange or red by severity, with red being the most serious.

stories.title: India's Commonwealth Games athletics campaign opens with a high-jump duel: Kushare vs Tejaswin
stories.what_happened: India's athletics campaign at the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow begins today with a three-way men's high jump final featuring Kushare, Shankar and Aadarsh Ram Jothi Shankar. It's the headline event of the day as India also has three weightlifting finals underway at the SEC Armadillo.
key_points: India's CWG 2026 athletics campaign in Glasgow opens today with the men's high jump final
National record holder Sarvesh Kushare faces former record holder Tejaswin Shankar
Kushare arrives on the back of a bronze at the Monaco Diamond League
Tejaswin won India's only CWG high-jump medal, bronze, at Birmingham 2022

depth.background: Tejaswin Shankar won India's only Commonwealth Games high-jump medal, a bronze, at Birmingham 2022, before shifting focus in recent years toward the decathlon. Sarvesh Kushare then broke Shankar's eight-year-old national record with a 2.31m leap in Bhubaneswar and has been in career-best form since, most recently taking bronze at the Monaco Diamond League.

stories.title: Government introduces a tougher anti-paper-leak bill in Lok Sabha as NEET fallout continues
stories.what_happened: Union Minister of State Jitendra Singh moved to introduce the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026 in the Lok Sabha today. The bill reportedly makes seven changes to the 2024 law, including strict time limits for both police investigations and court proceedings in paper-leak cases, aimed at closing enforcement gaps exposed by the NEET-UG case. Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju has urged MPs to take part in a full discussion on the bill, expected in the House tomorrow.
key_points: Union Minister Jitendra Singh introduces the Public Examinations Amendment Bill, 2026
It tightens the 2024 anti-paper-leak law with faster investigations and trials
Comes days after the education minister resigned over the NEET-UG leak row
Discussion on the bill is expected in the House tomorrow

depth.background: India passed the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act in 2024 to punish exam paper leaks and organised cheating rackets after a string of scandals. That law is now being tested by this year's alleged NEET-UG medical entrance exam leak, which triggered weeks of student protests, a police crackdown at a Delhi march, and the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan — replaced by Pralhad Joshi, as we reported yesterday. The government had promised tougher exam-security legislation as part of its response.

thread.previously: We reported that PM Modi had put Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani in charge of a new task force to reform India's exam system, alongside Modi announcing fast-track courts for the NEET paper-leak scandal.
thread.changed: Beyond task forces and courts, the government has now introduced actual legislation in Lok Sabha — the Public Examinations Amendment Bill, 2026 — to tighten the law itself, with a full debate expected tomorrow.
