stories.title: Modi tells his Cabinet: get on Instagram and start posting Reels for Gen Z
stories.what_happened: During a Union Cabinet meeting on Friday, Modi asked ministers how active they personally are on Instagram, and instructed them to make greater use of short-form videos and Reels to connect with young Indians. He reportedly said that simply posting updates about government schemes wasn't enough, and pushed ministers to communicate in a more interactive, relatable style, and to focus on platforms beyond X.
key_points: PM polled ministers in Friday's Cabinet meeting on their Instagram activity
Told them posting government updates isn't enough — engage youth directly, in a relatable way
Comes as Modi is the first world leader to cross 100 million Instagram followers
Signals a continued pivot toward reaching young voters where they scroll

depth.background: Indian politics has increasingly moved onto social media, and Modi has led that shift personally — he has built the largest Instagram following of any world leader. With protests over exam-paper leaks pulling in young people, the government is under pressure to be seen speaking to, not just about, India's youth.

stories.title: Russian missile hits a Ukrainian arms exhibition near Kyiv, killing at least 10 and injuring 100
stories.what_happened: On Friday, July 24, a Russian ballistic missile struck a training ground along the Zhytomyr Highway in the Kyiv region where an arms exhibition was underway, showcasing Ukrainian and foreign-made drones. At least 10 people were killed and more than 100 injured. Among the dead were Valentina Savitskaya, a senior Ukrainian state security official, and a colonel from Ukraine's security services. Russia's defense ministry said it deliberately targeted the exhibition, claiming the drones on display had been used to attack civilian sites inside Russia. President Zelensky condemned the strike as a deliberate attack on civilians.
key_points: A ballistic missile struck a defense-industry exhibition at a training ground near Kyiv
At least 10 killed, more than 100 injured, including senior Ukrainian security officials
Russia's defense ministry claimed responsibility, saying it targeted drone displays
Zelensky called it a 'brutal attack on civilians' and demanded accountability

depth.background: Russia and Ukraine have been at war since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Even amid periodic ceasefire talk elsewhere in the world, the two countries continue to trade long-range missile and drone strikes almost daily. Ukraine's defense industry has grown fast during the war, especially domestic drone-makers, and now regularly holds public exhibitions to showcase weapons to buyers and allies.

stories.title: England captain Nat Sciver-Brunt to sit out Trent Rockets' opening Hundred matches with calf trouble
stories.what_happened: Trent Rockets confirmed that captain Nat Sciver-Brunt will be unavailable for their opening two Hundred fixtures of the 2026 season, against Birmingham Phoenix and London Spirit, as she continues managing a calf injury first suffered playing domestic cricket in April. She is expected to return for the team's match in Cardiff the following Wednesday.
key_points: Sciver-Brunt will miss games against Birmingham Phoenix and London Spirit
She's managing a recurring calf injury that has bothered her all summer
She's set to return for Trent Rockets' trip to Cardiff next Wednesday
The injury already caused her to miss group games at the T20 World Cup this year

depth.background: The Hundred is England's short-format domestic cricket franchise league, running annually each summer with eight men's and women's teams. Nat Sciver-Brunt, England's white-ball captain and one of the world's leading all-rounders, has carried a nagging calf injury through much of the 2026 season, which already forced her out of parts of the T20 World Cup earlier this year.

stories.title: China's Nvidia challenger MetaX quietly files for a second listing in Hong Kong to fund its chip war
stories.what_happened: MetaX, a Shanghai-based designer of graphics processing units (GPUs, the specialized chips that power AI systems), has confidentially filed for a listing on the Hong Kong stock exchange, working with Huatai International on the share sale. The company is aiming to complete the IPO by the end of 2026. It plans to issue new Hong Kong-listed shares worth up to 5% of its enlarged share capital, on top of the roughly $600 million it already raised in a blockbuster Shanghai debut in December 2025.
key_points: MetaX has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO, targeting a listing by end of 2026
It's racing rivals Biren and Moore Threads to build China's homegrown alternative to Nvidia's AI chips
MetaX already raised about $600 million in a Shanghai listing in December 2025 that then jumped nearly 700% on debut
New funds are earmarked for next-generation GPU chips, software, supply chains and acquisitions

depth.background: The US has restricted sales of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China for national-security reasons, so Chinese tech firms can't just buy the best hardware on the market. Beijing has responded by pushing its own chipmakers, including MetaX, Biren and Moore Threads, to build competitive alternatives so the country's AI industry isn't dependent on American suppliers who could be cut off at any time.

stories.title: Fernando Alonso is now 'likely' to race on into 2027 — he doesn't want to retire on a 'sour note'
stories.what_happened: According to multiple reports this week, Alonso is now considered 'likely' to sign a new contract to continue racing into 2027, having decided he doesn't want to end his F1 career on a low note given Aston Martin's difficult 2026 season. Team principal Andy Cowell said he hasn't yet had direct conversations with Alonso about a 2027 deal, with their talks so far focused on getting through 2026.
key_points: Alonso, 45, is out of contract with Aston Martin at the end of 2026
Reports say he's now leaning toward signing on for 2027
Aston Martin says it hasn't yet discussed his future beyond 2026
He'd stay either as a driver or in a team-focused role

depth.background: Fernando Alonso is F1's oldest driver and a two-time world champion who joined Aston Martin in 2023 chasing a third title with the ambitious, Lawrence Stroll-owned team. Aston Martin's car has struggled through 2026, and Alonso had previously said publicly that a weak car might push him toward retirement rather than a 'one more year' decision.

stories.title: US swaps India's expiring 10% tariff for a new 'forced labour' tariff at the same rate
stories.what_happened: The 150-day Section 122 surcharge lapsed automatically at 12:01am US time on Friday, July 24, 2026. In its place, the US Trade Representative's office activated a new Section 301 tariff of 10% on Indian goods, citing forced-labour concerns, alongside 16 other countries including Bangladesh, Pakistan, Canada and the UK that also have forced-labour import bans. Countries without such bans, like China, Japan and the UK's non-exempt goods, face 12.5% instead. For India the net rate on affected goods stays at 10%, but on a different, more open-ended legal footing, stacking on top of existing Most-Favoured-Nation tariffs for sectors like textiles, gems, chemicals and engineering goods.
key_points: Old 10% US tariff on Indian goods expired at midnight July 24
Washington immediately replaced it with a new 10% 'forced labour' tariff
India got 10%, not 12.5%, after banning forced-labour-made imports on July 14
17 countries face 10%; China, Japan, UK face a steeper 12.5%

depth.background: In February 2026 the US imposed a temporary 10% across-the-board import surcharge (under a law called Section 122) on most trading partners, capped by law at 150 days. Separately, the US had opened a 'Section 301' probe into whether goods from 60 countries, including India, are made using forced labour, and floated tariffs of up to 12.5% on that basis. India moved on July 14 to amend its Foreign Trade Policy to formally ban imports made with forced labour, hoping to avoid the harsher rate.

stories.title: Adani denies plans to launch an airline — but reveals an $11 billion airport expansion instead
stories.what_happened: Adani Enterprises filed a stock-exchange disclosure on Thursday explicitly denying it is planning or evaluating entry into the commercial airline business, after earlier media reports said the group had approached the government about relaxing the ownership cap for airport operators. IndiGo's Rahul Bhatia publicly flagged the conflict-of-interest risk such a change would create. Separately, Adani's airport unit said it plans to invest more than $11 billion by 2030 to bid for close to a dozen new airport terminals, upgrade existing infrastructure and expand into aircraft maintenance — with Jeet Adani saying any IPO of the airport business depends on it first becoming cash-positive, with no fixed timeline yet.
key_points: Adani Enterprises told the stock exchange it is 'not evaluating' entering the commercial airline business, calling reports 'entirely baseless'
The denial follows reports Adani had asked the government to relax a rule capping airport operators at 10% ownership in a scheduled airline
IndiGo founder Rahul Bhatia warned of a 'conflict of interest' if an airport owner like Adani also ran an airline
Separately, Adani's airport unit plans to invest over $11 billion by 2030, bidding for nearly a dozen new terminals

depth.background: Adani Group already runs several of India's biggest airports, including Mumbai's, through its airport arm AAHL. Indian rules currently stop an airport operator from owning more than 10% of a scheduled airline, precisely to prevent the conflict of interest Bhatia flagged — an airport owner could otherwise favor its own airline with landing slots, gates or pricing over rivals like IndiGo and Air India. Reports that Adani had approached the government to loosen that rule triggered speculation the group was quietly preparing to enter aviation on both sides of the runway.

stories.title: Sudan's paramilitaries tighten a drone siege on El Obeid, leaving women to choose between attack by day and assault by night
stories.what_happened: UN Women and UN News reported that drone attacks on El Obeid have intensified to near-daily strikes as the RSF tries to impose a siege, hitting water points, power lines and fuel supplies. Residents describe having no safe time of day to fetch water. Separately, Sudan's army said it downed an advanced Chinese-made FH-95 drone near the city, the third such interception in July.
key_points: El Obeid — home to ~500,000 people plus 100,000 displaced — faces near-daily drone strikes
UN Women: daytime water runs risk drone strikes; night-time runs risk sexual assault
The RSF is targeting water, power and fuel infrastructure to force the city into submission
Sudan's army says it shot down a Chinese-made long-range drone nearby — its third interception this month

depth.background: Sudan's civil war began in April 2023 between the national army (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), splitting the country and triggering what aid groups call the world's largest displacement crisis. El Obeid, capital of North Kordofan state, is a key trading hub the army has held onto; the RSF besieged it before and broke through only briefly last year.

stories.title: Max Verstappen's contract 'escape clause' is about to unlock — and it could reshape F1's grid
stories.what_happened: Verstappen's contract with Red Bull runs through 2028, but reportedly includes a clause letting him leave for a rival as early as next season if certain performance conditions aren't met. With Red Bull's struggles continuing, that clause is expected to be triggered once Verstappen is mathematically unable to finish in the top two of this year's Drivers' Championship — a threshold expected to be crossed after this weekend's Hungarian Grand Prix. It has also emerged that Verstappen's management has held talks with McLaren about a possible future seat.
key_points: Verstappen is contracted to Red Bull through 2028, but a performance clause can free him early
The clause is expected to trigger once he can no longer finish top-two in the championship this weekend
Verstappen's camp has already spoken to McLaren about a possible future move
Fernando Alonso's own F1 future is separately expected to be decided this summer

depth.background: Red Bull has struggled with car performance this season, a steep fall for a team that dominated F1 for years with Verstappen, a four-time world champion. Top drivers' contracts sometimes include 'performance clauses' — conditions that let them exit early if the team fails to deliver a competitive car, protecting the driver from being stuck in an uncompetitive seat for years.

stories.title: F1 eyes a surprise Sepang return this year as a stand-in race, with Middle East races in doubt
stories.what_happened: F1 organizers are reportedly in talks with Sepang about a surprise return to the calendar this year as a replacement race, most likely slotting in on October 4, between the Azerbaijan Grand Prix and the Singapore Grand Prix. The move is being driven by concern that ongoing conflict in the Middle East could make it impossible to safely hold races there later in the season.
key_points: Sepang circuit reportedly the leading option to replace a cancelled race
Would slot in around October 4, between Baku and Singapore
Middle East conflict raises doubt over hosting races in Qatar/Abu Dhabi this season
Sepang hasn't hosted F1 since 2017, after a 19-season run

depth.background: Formula 1's calendar has long included multiple Middle East races, including Qatar and Abu Dhabi, usually as late-season fixtures. Sepang, in Malaysia, hosted F1 from 1999 to 2017 and was a fan-favorite circuit before it fell off the calendar over high hosting fees. The ongoing US-Iran war and its spread across the Gulf has put a question mark over whether it's safe or logistically possible to hold races in the region later this year.

stories.title: Gabriel Bortoleto shuts down 2027 exit talk: 'My future with Audi is already decided'
stories.what_happened: Speaking as the Hungarian Grand Prix weekend began, Bortoleto said, 'My future with Audi is already decided. I will remain with the team for many years. I have a multi-year contract,' pushing back on speculation about changes to the team's driver lineup for 2027.
key_points: Bortoleto says he has a multi-year contract and will stay with Audi 'for many years'
The Brazilian rookie's comments came as the Hungarian Grand Prix weekend got underway
He said he can't disclose the contract length but wouldn't object if Audi made it public
The statement shuts down speculation Audi could shake up its 2027 driver lineup

depth.background: Audi took over the former Sauber team's F1 entry this season as a full manufacturer effort, with Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg as its first pairing. As a new manufacturer investing heavily to become competitive, Audi's driver choices are watched closely — any hint of instability in the lineup fuels speculation given how much is riding on the project.

stories.title: Wall Street bounces back as Pakistan and China push a new plan to revive the collapsed US-Iran ceasefire talks
stories.what_happened: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Pakistani Deputy PM Ishaq Dar met in Shanghai and jointly called for an early ceasefire and a return to talks. Iran's interior minister also visited Islamabad twice in ten days for exploratory discussions. The proposal on the table would halt fighting and reopen shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — a critical oil chokepoint — while the US and Iran try to salvage their broader agreement. US stocks rose Friday and oil eased as traders read the diplomatic push as a reason the war might not escalate further, even though no formal deal has been reached.
key_points: Dow rose 0.7%, S&P 500 gained 0.5% Friday, clawing back Thursday's selloff
Oil eased back from near $100 a barrel on hopes of renewed diplomacy
Pakistan and China jointly called for the US and Iran to resume ceasefire talks
Neither Trump nor Iran has accepted the new proposal yet — fighting continues

depth.background: The US and Iran have been in an escalating conflict for months: a ceasefire broke down, US strikes on Iran have continued for nearly two weeks straight, and Iran-aligned Houthi fighters opened a second front by striking Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea — all of which pushed oil prices up and rattled stock markets on fears of a wider Middle East war. Pakistan, which has diplomatic channels to Tehran, and China, which has been courting a bigger regional role, have both been quietly trying to broker a way back to talks.

thread.previously: We covered the Houthis opening a new front by striking two Saudi oil tankers, escalating alongside the collapsing US-Iran ceasefire and pushing oil toward $100 a barrel.
thread.changed: Today, Pakistan and China are jointly pushing a new ceasefire proposal to get the US and Iran back to talks, and markets rallied on that hope — even though neither side has accepted it yet and fighting on the ground continues.

stories.title: West Indies pace bowler Alzarri Joseph turns down Test selection against Pakistan
stories.what_happened: A day after West Indies announced its Test squad to face Pakistan, head coach Daren Sammy confirmed that fast bowler Alzarri Joseph had actually declined his selection, contradicting Cricket West Indies' initial explanation that he was simply unavailable for personal reasons. Sammy said 'Mr Joseph has declined the selection' but did not reveal why, adding that resolving how contracted players can decline selection 'is a decision that is way over my head' and belongs to team directors.
key_points: Coach Daren Sammy confirms Joseph declined his spot, not just unavailable for 'personal reasons' as first said
Comes right after West Indies named its touring squad with a fresh face in the spin attack
Sammy says the decision is 'way over' his head, leaves it to team directors
The exact personal reasons behind the decision haven't been made public

depth.background: Cricket West Indies named its Test squad for the upcoming series against Pakistan just a day earlier, which included a new spin-bowling option as the team rebuilds its attack. West Indies contracts allow players some ability to decline selection, unlike at many other cricket boards, though it's unusual and puts selectors in an awkward spot.

thread.previously: West Indies named their Test squad to face Pakistan, notable for introducing a new spinner to the attack and naming a first-ever Test venue.
thread.changed: It's now confirmed that quick bowler Alzarri Joseph actually declined his spot in that squad, rather than simply being unavailable as first stated, leaving West Indies to fill the gap before the series.

prev_ref.title: West Indies name their Test squad for Pakistan, with a first-ever Test venue and a fresh face in the spin attack

stories.title: Crypto's fear gauge drops to 28 as Bitcoin slides under $65,000 — even as DeFi tokens surge 9.8%
stories.what_happened: Bitcoin fell roughly 1.4-1.8% to around $65,000 and Ethereum declined too, dragging the total crypto market capitalization down 1.3% to $2.3 trillion on $58.9 billion of trading volume. The Fear & Greed Index slid to 28, signaling traders are turning cautious again. The one outlier: DeFi tokens (cryptocurrencies tied to lending, trading and other financial apps built without banks) jumped 9.8%, suggesting money rotated into that corner of the market even as the majors sold off.
key_points: Total crypto market cap fell 1.3% to $2.3 trillion today
Bitcoin dropped to around $65,000, Ethereum fell too
The Fear & Greed Index — a 0-100 sentiment gauge — dropped to 28, deep in 'Fear' territory
DeFi (decentralized finance) tokens bucked the trend, surging 9.8%

depth.background: Crypto prices move heavily on sentiment, and traders track a 'Fear & Greed Index' that blends volatility, trading volume, social-media buzz and momentum into one number from 0 (Extreme Fear) to 100 (Extreme Greed). Bitcoin has been range-bound for weeks as investors debate whether the market has bottomed after a rough stretch, and the broader macro backdrop — a stock-market selloff, rising oil prices from the Iran conflict, and persistent uncertainty about interest rates — has kept risk appetite fragile across all speculative assets, not just crypto.

stories.title: Sweden fast-tracks mining permits to break China's grip on rare-earth elements
stories.what_happened: Sweden announced it wants to accelerate approval of mining permits for its rare-earth deposits, formalizing this as a national-security priority in a July 2026 declaration, explicitly framed as helping the European Union reduce its dependence on China. Sweden holds some of Europe's largest known rare-earth deposits.
key_points: Sweden wants to speed up permits to mine rare earths
China controls roughly 70% of world rare-earth mining
Move backed by a new July 2026 national-security declaration
Mines typically take 10-15 years to build even on a fast track

depth.background: Rare-earth elements are a group of 17 metals essential for magnets used in EV motors, wind turbines, smartphones and missile-guidance systems. China dominates their mining and, even more, their processing — refining raw ore into usable material — giving it outsized leverage in trade disputes. Earlier in 2026 China tightened export controls on rare earths and related dual-use items (goods with both civilian and military uses), rattling manufacturers worldwide who depend on Chinese supply.

stories.title: Cricket Australia says it's open to playing an Ashes Test in India — a first for the 143-year-old rivalry
stories.what_happened: Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg told BBC Sport the board is willing to seriously explore staging an Ashes Test in India, calling it 'worth exploring' given CA's strong relationships with both the ECB and BCCI. He stressed it isn't currently planned and would require both boards to agree.
key_points: CA chief Todd Greenberg says India hosting is 'worth exploring'
The Ashes has never been played outside Australia or England
Would need BCCI and ECB sign-off — not planned near-term
Follows a CA-BCCI deal to host a Big Bash League match in Chennai

depth.background: The Ashes, first played in 1882, is Test cricket's oldest and most storied rivalry, contested only between Australia and England, always on their own soil. India is by far cricket's biggest commercial market, and boards around the world have increasingly looked to schedule marquee content there — Cricket Australia and the BCCI recently agreed to stage a Big Bash League game in Chennai.

stories.title: Assam's flood death toll climbs to 50 as 700,000 people are displaced and Guwahati's roads go under
stories.what_happened: Assam's flood death toll has risen to at least 50, up from 36 the day before, with 700,000 people now displaced after days of heavy monsoon rain overflowed the Brahmaputra. Nearly 900 villages have been submerged and more than 7,000 homes lost power. Almost 300,000 people are now in government relief camps. Flooding on Thursday evening disrupted Guwahati, Assam's capital and home to about 2 million people, leaving commuters stranded on submerged roads for hours. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said authorities are running relief operations including helicopter airdrops of food and supplies.
key_points: Death toll now at least 50, up from 36 a day earlier
700,000 people displaced; nearly 300,000 in relief camps
Almost 900 villages submerged by the overflowing Brahmaputra river
State capital Guwahati (2 million people) had roads flood Thursday evening, stranding commuters

depth.background: Assam sits on the floodplain of the Brahmaputra, one of Asia's largest rivers, which starts in Tibet and flows nearly 900 km through the state. Heavy monsoon rain every year swells the river past its banks, and this year's monsoon has been especially severe — deaths and displacement have been climbing steadily through the week as more districts get hit.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported the Assam floods had killed 36 people for the week and affected 650,000 across 11 districts, with the toll climbing daily.
thread.changed: The death toll has risen to at least 50 and displacement to 700,000, and the flooding has now reached the state capital Guwahati itself, disrupting roads and stranding commuters for the first time.

stories.title: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka get a straight run to the Asian Games cricket knockouts
stories.what_happened: The International Cricket Council and Asian Games organizers confirmed that India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, as the region's top-ranked sides, will go straight into the men's cricket quarterfinals at the 2026 Asian Games, skipping the preliminary rounds entirely. The 10-team men's competition begins September 24 in Nagoya, Japan, with Afghanistan, Japan and Nepal in one preliminary group and Hong Kong, Malaysia and Oman in the other; the top two from each group join the four seeded teams in the quarterfinals. The women's tournament, held September 17-22 with eight teams, also starts directly at the quarterfinal stage, pairing defending champions India against hosts Japan, Bangladesh against China, Sri Lanka against Malaysia, and Pakistan against Thailand.
key_points: Four top-ranked sides skip the group stage and go directly to the men's quarterfinals
10-team tournament starts September 24 in Nagoya, Japan
Afghanistan, Japan and Nepal in one preliminary group; Hong Kong, Malaysia and Oman in the other
Women's event runs September 17-22 with 8 teams starting straight at the quarterfinal stage

depth.background: Cricket returned to the Asian Games program in 2023 after a long absence, giving the sport an Olympic-style multi-sport stage in Asia. Not every cricket-playing Asian nation has equal playing strength, so organizers seed the strongest teams directly into the knockout rounds while weaker sides play a preliminary group stage to earn the remaining spots.

stories.title: A West Bank shooting near Nablus kills an Israeli and four Palestinians, and Netanyahu vows a hard response
stories.what_happened: On Friday morning, Palestinians attacked a group of Israeli hikers near the Havat Gilad settlement outpost west of Nablus, seizing a weapon from a civilian security coordinator and opening fire. A 32-year-old Israeli man, Benayahu Melet, was killed trying to help the hikers. In the gunfight and clashes that followed, four Palestinians were also killed and several more people on both sides were wounded.
key_points: Palestinians attacked Israeli hikers near the Havat Gilad settlement, seizing a weapon
An Israeli civilian, 32, was killed helping the hikers; four Palestinians died in the ensuing gunfight
Settler groups launched retaliatory raids on nearby Palestinian villages
Netanyahu convened his defense minister and army chief to plan a response

depth.background: The West Bank has been on edge for years as Jewish settlements expand into land Palestinians want for a future state, and violence between settlers, Palestinian residents, and Israeli security forces has become a near-weekly occurrence. Havat Gilad is one of dozens of unauthorized settler outposts Israel has increasingly moved to formalize, which Palestinians see as land theft. Attacks like this one happen against the backdrop of the wider, unresolved Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the ongoing war in Gaza.

stories.title: Mercedes says it's found what was sabotaging George Russell's power unit — a hidden software bug
stories.what_happened: Mercedes' investigation found the cause of Russell's power deployment issues was a deeply embedded calibration bug in the power unit's control software — not a hardware failure. Russell said it was 'almost impossible to see unless you knew exactly what to look for.' The team has recalibrated the relevant software parameters ahead of the Hungarian Grand Prix, though it won't get true confirmation the fix worked until the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, because Hungary's track doesn't replicate the high-speed conditions where the bug showed up.
key_points: Mercedes traces Russell's power struggles to a deeply buried calibration error, not a hardware fault
The issue robbed him of straight-line speed and cost him over half a second at Spa
Team believes it has recalibrated the software fix in time for the Hungarian GP
Full confirmation won't come until Monza, since Hungary's track doesn't stress the same systems

depth.background: George Russell is Mercedes' lead driver, racing alongside rookie sensation Kimi Antonelli. Modern F1 power units are hybrid systems where software decides exactly how and when to deploy electric boost alongside the combustion engine — meaning a bug in that code can cripple a car's performance even if every physical part is fine. Russell had a miserable weekend at Spa (Belgium), qualifying more than half a second slower than his teammate Antonelli despite comparable equipment.

stories.title: Assam's monsoon floods turn catastrophic — at least 50 dead, 700,000 displaced as the Brahmaputra overflows
stories.what_happened: Assam's government said Friday that ongoing flooding has now killed at least 50 people and displaced roughly 700,000, with about 300,000 people now in relief camps, after days of heavy monsoon rain overflowed the Brahmaputra river. Nearly 900 villages are submerged and more than 7,000 homes are without electricity. On Thursday evening the flooding reached Guwahati, Assam's capital of about 2 million people, leaving commuters stranded for hours on submerged roads. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said authorities are running helicopter airdrops of food and relief supplies to cut-off areas.
key_points: At least 50 people killed and 700,000 displaced across Assam
The Brahmaputra river overflowed after days of relentless monsoon rain
Nearly 900 villages submerged, over 7,000 homes without power
Guwahati, Assam's 2-million-person capital, saw commuters stranded for hours as roads went underwater

depth.background: The Brahmaputra is one of Asia's biggest rivers, flowing about 900 km through Assam after originating in Tibet. Assam floods most monsoon seasons (June–September) because the river's banks can't hold sudden surges of Himalayan meltwater and heavy rain; this year's monsoon had already killed at least 25 people across India's north in mid-July before this fresh escalation.

thread.previously: We reported that India's monsoon had turned deadly, with cloudbursts and floods killing dozens and displacing thousands.
thread.changed: The toll has surged specifically in Assam: at least 50 dead and 700,000 displaced as the Brahmaputra river overflowed and floodwaters reached the state capital, Guwahati.

stories.title: Wildfires force 44,000 to flee in France and Spain as the EU rushes in firefighting planes
stories.what_happened: Fast-moving wildfires, fueled by extreme heat, drought and strong winds, swept through southwestern France near Bordeaux and parts of Spain and Italy this week. In France, roughly 44,000 people have been evacuated over the past two days and 12,500 hectares of forest destroyed, with more than 25,000 forced from campsites and holiday homes along the Atlantic coast. Spain declared a national emergency as blazes merged outside Madrid, and both countries requested help through the EU's Civil Protection Mechanism. The EU is sending four firefighting aircraft to Spain and three to France, including Croatian and Portuguese planes, Czech and Slovak heavy-lift helicopters, and Italian and Greek water-dumping aircraft.
key_points: Southwestern France: 44,000 evacuated in two days, 12,500 hectares burned
Spain declares a national emergency as blazes merge near Madrid
EU's Civil Protection Mechanism sends Croatian, Portuguese, Italian and Greek aircraft plus Czech/Slovak helicopters
Extreme heat, drought and strong winds are driving the fires

depth.background: Southern Europe has faced worsening summer wildfire seasons for years as heatwaves grow more frequent and intense. When a country's own firefighting capacity is overwhelmed, EU members can request help through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, a system that pools aircraft, vehicles and personnel from other member states.

stories.title: F1 stewards admit they got the Leclerc-Piastri Spa crash wrong
stories.what_happened: At a long-planned drivers' meeting with FIA stewards at the Hungarian Grand Prix on Thursday night, officials accepted they made a mistake at Spa and that Leclerc 'likely' should have received a five-second time penalty for the move that damaged Piastri's car. Stewards indicated that, going forward, a similar squeeze on a rival at corner entry would typically draw that penalty. Leclerc maintained the incident wasn't clear-cut, while Piastri argued that letting it go unpunished set a bad precedent for how tightly drivers can race.
key_points: Stewards privately conceded Leclerc likely deserved a 5-second penalty for squeezing Piastri at Spa
Admission came at a scheduled drivers-FIA meeting in Hungary on Thursday night
Lewis Hamilton reportedly skipped the meeting
Piastri had pushed back on setting a precedent that squeezing a rival that tightly is acceptable

depth.background: At the Belgian Grand Prix, Charles Leclerc squeezed Oscar Piastri at the Les Combes corner and the two made contact, damaging Piastri's McLaren floor; stewards judged it a racing incident at the time and issued no penalty. F1 holds regular meetings between drivers and race stewards to iron out how the rules are applied consistently.

stories.title: F1's biggest driver-market shock could land this weekend as Verstappen and Piastri's exit clauses both hinge on the Hungary summer break
stories.what_happened: Multiple F1 outlets report that Max Verstappen's Red Bull contract contains a performance-linked exit clause — requiring him to be inside the top two or three in the drivers' standings by this weekend's summer break — and that he currently sits 7th, roughly 78 points behind George Russell in 2nd, well outside that bar. Oscar Piastri's McLaren contract reportedly has a similar clause requiring a top-five finish by the same deadline. Because both deadlines land at the same moment — right after Sunday's Hungarian Grand Prix — paddock reporters are describing the next 72 hours as a potential flashpoint where one or both drivers' long-term futures get decided.
key_points: Verstappen's Red Bull deal reportedly lets him leave if he's outside the top 2-3 in the standings by the summer break
He's currently 7th, about 78 points off Russell in 2nd — squarely outside the trigger zone
Piastri's McLaren contract has a separate clause tied to being outside the top 5 by the same deadline
The summer break starts right after Sunday's race, creating a ~72-hour window where both futures could be decided

depth.background: F1 teams sometimes write performance-based exit clauses into multi-year driver contracts — if a driver falls short of an agreed championship position by a set date, they can walk away early. Verstappen signed a long-term Red Bull deal (through 2028) after his multiple championship years, but Red Bull's car has struggled to keep pace this season, and Verstappen is reported to be increasingly frustrated with the team. Piastri, meanwhile, is under contract at McLaren through 2028 but has a separate clause of his own. The 'summer break' is F1's mandatory factory shutdown after the Hungarian Grand Prix, traditionally the moment silly-season rumors either fizzle or turn into real announcements.

stories.title: Teen Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's record 18-ball fifty fires India past Zimbabwe, ending a rough T20I run
stories.what_happened: Batting after Zimbabwe were put in and made 125-7 in 20 overs, 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi smashed four sixes and four fours in an 18-ball fifty — the youngest half-century in international T20 cricket. India cruised to 126-3 with 40 balls unused, with wicketkeeper Ishan Kishan (35) and captain Shreyas Iyer (28 not out) also contributing, to win the first of three T20Is by 7 wickets.
key_points: 15-year-old Sooryavanshi hits a fifty off just 18 balls
It's the youngest half-century in international T20 history
India wins the 1st T20I by 7 wickets, chasing 126 with 40 balls to spare
Comes after India was swept 0-2 by Ireland and 0-4 by England

depth.background: India's T20I side, now led by new captain Shreyas Iyer, had been through a miserable recent run — swept 2-0 by Ireland and then 4-0 by England — heading into a three-match tour of Zimbabwe.

stories.title: India-US interim tariff deal expires today with no pact signed, as talks go down to the wire
stories.what_happened: With the July 24 deadline arriving, India and the US have not signed the interim Bilateral Trade Agreement both sides have been negotiating. Reports describe the text as parked at the 'last 1%,' with both sides still working through details — including new US tariff threats on imported medicines that concern India's large pharmaceutical export industry. India's negotiators say they are prioritizing favorable terms relative to competing Asian exporters over meeting the calendar deadline.
key_points: Temporary US tariff arrangement on Indian goods expires today, July 24
No signed trade pact yet — deal reportedly stuck on the 'last 1%' of legal text
India pushing for tariff parity with rival Asian exporters, not a rushed deal
Pharma tariff threats are a key sticking point

depth.background: The US and India have spent months negotiating an interim trade pact to head off a bigger US tariff increase on Indian exports. The Trump administration has been using tariff threats broadly this year — including a global emergency tariff — as leverage in trade talks with dozens of countries. For India, the stakes include a temporary 10% tariff arrangement that was due to lapse today, after which Indian goods could face the higher 'most-favoured-nation' (MFN) rates that apply by default.

stories.title: Iran fires drones at US bases in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan as its retaliation spreads across the Gulf
stories.what_happened: Iran's army said Friday it launched drone strikes against several US military facilities in Bahrain and Jordan, adding to strikes it had already carried out on bases in Kuwait, in retaliation for the latest round of US bombing inside Iran. The move broadens the list of Gulf host nations being hit — countries that host US troops but are not themselves parties to the war. It came hours after the US military completed its 13th consecutive night of strikes on Iranian targets, with President Trump signaling a ceasefire is not imminent.
key_points: Iran's military says it struck US facilities in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan overnight
It's the widest spread yet of Iran's retaliation — earlier strikes had mostly hit Qatar and Saudi Arabia
Comes hours after the US carried out its 13th straight night of strikes on Iran
Trump says he is 'close to' ordering a 'massive attack', bigger than anything so far

depth.background: The US and Iran have been trading direct military blows for nearly five months, after talks over Iran's nuclear program collapsed and the US began bombing Iranian nuclear and military sites. Iran has retaliated by firing drones and missiles at the US military bases that dot the Gulf — Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and now Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan all host American troops and are within range of Iranian weapons.

stories.title: Mumbai's trains grind to a halt in heavy rain, as police ban protests over the NEET paper leak through August 6
stories.what_happened: Heavy rain over July 23-24 disrupted Mumbai-bound rail traffic, forcing cancellation of marquee trains including Vande Bharat and Shatabdi services on the Mumbai-Ahmedabad route, alongside widespread local commuter disruption. Separately, Mumbai Police used Section 144 — a legal provision banning public gatherings — to prohibit protests city-wide from July 23 through August 6, specifically targeting demonstrations tied to the NEET paper-leak issue.
key_points: Heavy monsoon rain cancels Vande Bharat, Shatabdi and other long-distance trains
Mumbai under a Yellow Alert; a key reservoir near 70% capacity
Police impose Section 144 (public-gathering ban) in Mumbai from July 23 to August 6
Ban aimed at ongoing NEET paper-leak protests

depth.background: India's monsoon (the seasonal rains that run roughly June to September) has been unusually intense this year, and Mumbai — a coastal city whose suburban and long-distance rail network is its commuting backbone — is especially vulnerable to flooding and service disruption. Separately, protests have built for weeks over alleged leaks of the NEET medical-entrance exam paper, a scandal that has already forced out the government's Higher Education Secretary and fueled demands the education minister resign.

stories.title: Bangladesh's President Shahabuddin resigns citing health, as pressure grows over Hasina's planned return
stories.what_happened: Shahabuddin announced his resignation on Friday, saying newly diagnosed autonomic neuropathy causes him to occasionally lose consciousness. The announcement came a day after reports that he was being pushed to resign specifically because of growing pressure linked to Hasina's planned return to Bangladesh. Under the constitution, the speaker of parliament takes over presidential duties until a new president is elected within 90 days.
key_points: President Mohammed Shahabuddin, 76, resigned Friday citing a nerve condition (autonomic neuropathy)
He quits nearly two years before his term was due to end in 2028
Comes amid mounting pressure tied to ousted PM Sheikh Hasina's planned return from exile
Parliament's speaker takes over the ceremonial role; a new president must be chosen within 90 days

depth.background: Bangladesh has been in near-constant political upheaval since a student-led uprising ousted long-time Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in 2024, forcing her into exile in India. Shahabuddin, whose presidency is largely ceremonial, had been under pressure for months over his past ties to the Hasina government, with critics accusing him of quietly protecting her interests.

stories.title: India's factories and services hire at the fastest pace in nearly 20 years, PMI shows — even as the stock market slides
stories.what_happened: S&P Global/HSBC's flash India Composite PMI climbed to 61.4 in July from June's final 60.9, driven by strong services demand (PMI 61.1) and a pickup in manufacturing (58.5, the highest since April). Companies reported hiring at the fastest pace since April 2006 as order books grew.
key_points: HSBC flash India Composite PMI rose to 61.4 in July, a 3-month high
Services PMI hit a 4-month high of 61.1; manufacturing rose to 58.5
Job creation grew at its fastest pace since April 2006
Comes even as Sensex and Nifty fall for a fifth straight day

depth.background: The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a monthly survey of company managers that gauges whether business activity is expanding or shrinking — a reading above 50 means growth. India's PMI has stayed above 50 for roughly three straight years, one of the strongest expansion streaks of any major economy, even as global growth has cooled.

stories.title: India's Commonwealth Games campaign hit by doping scandal before it even starts — two athletes withdrawn
stories.what_happened: India's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) said Arun Kumar failed an out-of-competition test, returning an adverse finding for an anabolic steroid. He's been handed a provisional suspension and ruled ineligible for Glasgow. Weightlifter Dilbagh Singh has also been withdrawn from the Games in the same doping-related sweep. The Indian judo team was due to fly out on July 27.
key_points: Judoka Arun Kumar tests positive for an anabolic steroid, pulled from Glasgow squad
Weightlifter Dilbagh Singh also withdrawn in the same doping sweep
NADA's out-of-competition test caught Kumar; he gets a provisional suspension
Rules mean India can't even name a replacement for his weight category

depth.background: India had been building toward the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow (starting July 31) with real medal hopes across boxing, judo, weightlifting and para-sports — several Indian athletes, including Lovlina Borgohain, already have upcoming medal shots lined up. Judoka Arun Kumar, 21, competing in the men's 73kg category, had a strong recent run: gold at the Taipei Asian Open in 2025 and a start at the Qingdao Grand Prix last month.

stories.title: India dodges the higher tariff bracket as the old US tariff deal expires — lands 10%, not 12.5%
stories.what_happened: The 10% temporary US tariff on Indian exports expired at 9:31am IST today. Rather than a full signed trade deal, the US instead issued new tariff slabs under its Section 301 trade law, initially expected to put India in a 12.5% bracket — but after last-minute discussions on labor practices, India secured the lower 10% rate instead. That relief applies to roughly 92% of India's $87.2 billion in annual merchandise exports to the US, which return to normal, most-favoured-nation tariff rates. No comprehensive deal text has been signed or published.
key_points: The temporary 10% US tariff on Indian goods expired at 9:31am IST today
Washington's new tariff slabs put India in the lower 10% bracket, not the initially-planned 12.5%
About 92% of India's $87.2 billion in US-bound exports return to normal WTO tariff rates
A full India-US trade deal is still NOT signed — this is just today's tariff reset

depth.background: For months, India and the US have been racing to finalize a bilateral trade agreement before a temporary US tariff arrangement expired. As of yesterday, negotiators were still stuck on the 'last one percent' of the legal text — sticking points included how much of a tariff edge India gets over rivals like Vietnam, and US demands for guarantees that Indian supply chains (textiles, seafood, manufacturing) are free of forced labor.

thread.previously: We reported the deal was stuck at the 'last one percent' of legal text, with the tariff deadline just hours away and no resolution in sight.
thread.changed: The deadline has now passed — no full deal was signed, but India secured a better-than-expected outcome: a 10% tariff rate instead of the 12.5% initially floated, sparing most of its US-bound exports.

stories.title: India's paper-leak protest movement calls a nationwide strike today, as Delhi Metro shuts stations for a third straight day
stories.what_happened: The CJP called for peaceful protests in every district of the country today, urging supporters to gather locally, read out their demands, and show solidarity with students and others injured in the July 20 police action. In Delhi, the metro operator shut 17 stations for a third consecutive day as security was tightened around the ongoing sit-in, and CJP representatives are meeting central government officials today to discuss the demonstration's terms.
key_points: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called protests in 'every district' today under the slogan 'one day, one demand'
Delhi Metro shut 17 stations today — the third straight day of closures around the protest site
CJP holds talks with the Centre today over the terms and venue for its demonstration
Core demand: Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the NEET paper leak, plus accountability for injuries during police action

depth.background: The Cockroach Janta Party is a youth-led protest movement that grew out of anger over a leaked question paper for NEET, India's national medical-entrance exam, which millions of students sit every year. The movement escalated after police action against a 'Chalo Sansad' (march to Parliament) protest on July 20 left a student protester seriously injured, and activist Sonam Wangchuk had just ended a 26-day hunger strike in solidarity days before this call for a nationwide strike.

stories.title: Ukraine's homemade Flamingo missile hits a Russian weapons plant 1,200 km from the border
stories.what_happened: Ukrainian forces struck the Avitek defense plant in the Russian city of Kirov early on July 24 using a Flamingo cruise missile, according to Ukraine's military and confirmed by Fire Point, the missile's manufacturer. Kirov sits about 1,200 km (750 miles) from the Ukrainian border. Russian authorities reported at least six people killed and dozens injured; a central building at the plant was hit and fires broke out.
key_points: Flamingo cruise missile struck the Avitek defense plant in Kirov, Russia
Kirov is nearly 750 miles inside Russia — one of Ukraine's deepest strikes yet
Plant makes ejection seats and parts for Russian missiles
At least 6 killed, dozens hurt in the strike

depth.background: Ukraine's home-built Flamingo cruise missile, unveiled in 2025, is one of the longest-range weapons Kyiv has ever fielded — reportedly able to fly around 3,000 km with a heavy warhead, and built entirely in Ukraine so it faces none of the usage restrictions that come with Western-supplied weapons. Through 2026, Kyiv has increasingly aimed at Russia's ability to build and sustain its war machine — factories, refineries, and airfields far from the front line — rather than only contesting territory.

thread.previously: Yesterday, Ukraine sent 223 drones roughly 400 miles into Russia, hitting an oil refinery and a major e-commerce logistics hub as part of a deliberate economic-pressure campaign.
thread.changed: Today Ukraine went nearly three times deeper — 1,200 km — using a homemade Flamingo cruise missile to hit a defense plant that makes ejection seats and missile components, a military rather than economic target.

prev_ref.title: Ukraine sends 223 drones deep into Russia overnight, hitting an oil refinery and 'Russia's Amazon'

stories.title: Russia fires over 100 drones and missiles at Ukraine overnight, killing two people in a Donetsk apartment strike
stories.what_happened: Russia launched more than 100 drones and several missiles at Ukraine overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying most were Iranian-made Shahed drones. A strike hit residential and commercial buildings in Kostyantynivka, killing two people and injuring 14, and damaging five apartment blocks, eight houses, shops and vehicles.
key_points: Russia launched 100+ strike drones (mostly Iranian-designed Shaheds) and 4+ missiles overnight into July 24
A strike on Kostyantynivka, in Ukraine's Donetsk region, killed 2 people and injured 14
Five apartment buildings, 8 houses, shops and vehicles were damaged
The attack came as fighting continued along the front line with no ceasefire in place

depth.background: Kostyantynivka is a front-line town in Donetsk that Russian forces have been grinding toward for months — Russian President Vladimir Putin has even falsely claimed at times to have already captured it, which independent analysts say overstates Russia's actual, much slower progress. Overnight mass-drone-and-missile barrages like this one have become Russia's routine method of pressuring Ukrainian cities and infrastructure while ground fighting continues in the east.

stories.title: China's central bank pumps extra cash into banks as new US tariffs bite
stories.what_happened: On Friday, the PBOC announced a 500-billion-yuan one-year MLF operation, conducted through a variable-rate, fixed-quantity, multiple-price auction. With 400 billion yuan of existing MLF loans maturing this month, the operation works out to a net injection of 100 billion yuan of fresh liquidity into the banking system — the third consecutive month the PBOC has increased this rollover, and per Bloomberg the largest liquidity addition in five months.
key_points: PBOC to run a 500-billion-yuan (~$73.9B) one-year lending operation
Old loans maturing this month total 400 billion yuan — a 100-billion-yuan net top-up
Third straight month the PBOC has increased this kind of rollover
Comes as new US tariffs of 10-12.5% on 60 countries, including China, take effect

depth.background: China's central bank, the People's Bank of China (PBOC), regularly lends money to commercial banks for about a year at a time through a tool called the Medium-term Lending Facility (MLF), to keep credit flowing through the economy. It has been gradually increasing how much new money it adds each month as China's export-driven economy faces fresh pressure from US trade measures.

stories.title: US completes a 13th straight night of strikes on Iran as Tehran rejects an Iraq-brokered ceasefire
stories.what_happened: US Central Command carried out its 13th consecutive night of strikes on Iran, hitting military command centers, drone storage facilities, communications networks, coastal surveillance sites, and assets Iran could use against ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The strikes wrapped up around 9pm US Eastern time. State media said at least four people were killed. Separately, Iran rejected a ceasefire proposal that Iraq's prime minister had carried to Tehran on Washington's behalf — Iranian officials said they would not accept any deal that left control of the Strait unresolved. President Trump said Thursday that Iran needs 'more of the same,' signaling no near-term pause.
key_points: US hit Iranian command centers, drone storage sites and coastal radar for the 13th consecutive night
Iran rejected a temporary ceasefire relayed by Iraq's prime minister
Sticking point: who controls the Strait of Hormuz, the oil chokepoint
Trump says Iran needs 'more of the same' — no truce signaled

depth.background: The US and Iran have been in an escalating shadow war for months, triggered by Iran targeting tankers and infrastructure near the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through. Washington has responded with nightly airstrikes rather than a single knockout campaign, betting that sustained pressure forces Tehran back to the table. Iraq, which borders both the US's regional partners and Iran, has been quietly shuttling ceasefire proposals between the two sides.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Trump's threat to strike Iranian infrastructure — a bridge or power plant — every time Iran fired on a ship near Hormuz, as the ceasefire that had briefly held collapsed.
thread.changed: That threat has become a sustained campaign: a 13th straight night of US strikes, a rejected Iraqi-mediated ceasefire offer, and Trump saying Iran needs 'more of the same' — the confrontation has hardened rather than cooled.

prev_ref.title: Trump vows to bomb an Iranian bridge or power plant every time Iran fires on a ship in the Strait of Hormuz

stories.title: Trump rolls out new 10–12.5% tariffs on 60 countries over 'forced labor' — the replacement for the tariffs the Supreme Court struck down
stories.what_happened: Those new tariffs took effect on July 24, 2026. They use a different law — Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which lets a president retaliate against 'unfair trade practices' — instead of the law the Supreme Court struck down. US trade investigators concluded all 60 partners had failed to adequately block forced-labor goods, triggering duties of 10% (for countries that have at least banned such imports on paper) or 12.5% (for those that haven't). Together the 60 countries account for 99.4% of US trade.
key_points: New tariffs of 10% or 12.5% now apply to goods from 60 countries, covering over 99% of all US imports
Legal basis this time is a forced-labor law (Section 301), not the emergency powers law the Supreme Court rejected in February
Countries get the lower 10% rate if they've banned forced-labor imports, 12.5% if they haven't
Trade partners are furious and legal challenges have already been filed

depth.background: In February 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that Trump's original 'Liberation Day' tariffs were illegal — the emergency-powers law he used (called IEEPA) doesn't actually let a president impose tariffs, the Court said. That should have ended the blanket tariffs. Instead, the administration spent months building a legal workaround: investigations into whether America's 60 biggest trading partners were doing enough to stop goods made with forced labor from entering their supply chains.

thread.previously: Yesterday's story reported that Trump's original blanket 10% tariff was expiring by law and that a replacement was already being prepared.
thread.changed: That replacement is now live: a 60-country, forced-labor-justified tariff regime took effect July 24, using a different law than the one the Supreme Court struck down.

stories.title: Trump's blanket 10% global tariff expires by law — and a replacement is already coming
stories.what_happened: The Section 122 tariff — a flat 10% surcharge applied to most goods entering the US — expired automatically by law at 12:01am Eastern time on July 24, 2026, exactly 150 days after it took effect. Extending it further would require an act of Congress, and no such bill is pending. Trade lawyers say the administration is expected to announce replacement duties in the coming days under other legal authorities (Section 301 or Section 232), which could preserve, narrow, or even raise tariffs on specific countries and products.
key_points: The Section 122 tariff — a 10% duty on nearly all imports — expired at 12:01am July 24
It was a temporary fix after courts struck down Trump's earlier tariff plan
The law only allows this kind of emergency tariff for 150 days, with no renewal without Congress
The administration is expected to announce replacement tariffs under different legal powers within days

depth.background: Earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down the sweeping import tariffs Trump had imposed using emergency economic powers (the IEEPA law), ruling he'd overstepped his authority. In response, the administration switched to a different, narrower legal tool — 'Section 122' of the Trade Act of 1974 — which lets a president impose an import surcharge of up to 15% for a maximum of 150 days without needing Congress's approval, as a stopgap while a longer-term trade fix is worked out. That 150-day clock started February 24.

stories.title: Brazil denies visas to two US officials seeking to scrutinize its election, deepening a trade-and-politics rift with Washington
stories.what_happened: Brazil's government denied visa requests from two US State Department officials, Riley M. Barnes and Samuel Samson, who had planned to travel to Brazil to scrutinize the fairness of its electoral system ahead of the October presidential vote. The officials applied for visas on July 20; Brazil turned them down on Friday, July 24. Brazilian officials, speaking anonymously, said they saw the planned visit as an attempt to interfere in the election.
key_points: Brazil rejected visa requests from two senior US State Department officials who wanted to examine its electoral system
The officials — assistant secretary Riley Barnes and deputy assistant Samuel Samson — applied on July 20; Brazil said no on Friday
Brazilian officials call it attempted election interference, just over two months before Brazil's October 4 presidential vote
It lands the same week Washington imposed tariffs of up to 37.5% on thousands of Brazilian exports

depth.background: Brazil and the US have been at odds for months over trade and diplomacy, with Washington repeatedly using tariffs as leverage. Brazil goes to the polls on October 4, 2026, to pick its next president, in a race being watched closely for outside interference — a charge Brazil is now leveling squarely at the US.

stories.title: HCLTech signs ₹14,257 crore deal to build a sovereign AI data centre in Odisha with Sarvam
stories.what_happened: HCLTech signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Sarvam and the Odisha state government to build an AI-optimised data centre in the upcoming Odisha Sovereign Park in Bhubaneswar, with a planned outlay of about ₹14,257 crore. Alongside the data centre, HCLTech will set up a global delivery centre in the state, expected to create around 5,000 jobs; the facility is targeted to begin operations by 2028.
key_points: HCLTech, AI startup Sarvam, and the Odisha government signed an MoU for an AI data centre in Bhubaneswar
Planned investment: about ₹14,257 crore (roughly $1.4 billion)
HCLTech will also build a delivery centre creating around 5,000 jobs in the state
Facility is expected to start operating by 2028

depth.background: A 'data centre' is a huge warehouse full of specialized computer chips (GPUs) that train and run AI models — without enough of this computing power, a country or company can't build or run advanced AI. India currently relies heavily on foreign cloud providers for this compute, and the government has been pushing 'sovereign AI' — domestically located, domestically controlled AI infrastructure. HCLTech is one of India's largest IT services companies; Sarvam is a well-funded Indian AI startup building foundation models tailored to Indian languages.

stories.title: BNP Paribas Cardif to buy a 26% stake in IndiaFirst Life from Warburg Pincus
stories.what_happened: BNP Paribas Cardif signed a definitive agreement on July 24 to acquire Warburg Pincus's roughly 26% stake in IndiaFirst Life Insurance, at a valuation of about ₹10,000 crore for the company. The deal still needs clearance from India's insurance regulator, IRDAI, before it can close.
key_points: French insurer BNP Paribas Cardif is buying Warburg Pincus's ~26% stake in IndiaFirst Life
The deal values IndiaFirst Life at roughly ₹10,000 crore (about $1.2 billion)
Bank of Baroda remains IndiaFirst Life's majority owner
It marks BNP Paribas Cardif's return to India's fast-growing life insurance market

depth.background: IndiaFirst Life is a life insurer majority-owned by Bank of Baroda, a large Indian public-sector bank, with private equity firm Warburg Pincus and Union Bank of India holding other stakes. Private equity firms like Warburg Pincus invest in companies to grow them over several years, then look to sell ('exit') to realize returns. BNP Paribas Cardif is the insurance arm of French banking giant BNP Paribas.

stories.title: Oman sends a delegation to Tehran to try to keep ships moving safely through the Strait of Hormuz
stories.what_happened: An Omani diplomatic delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday to discuss arrangements for the safe passage of commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also spoke by phone with Oman's foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, about regional security and vessel movement through the strait and the wider Persian Gulf.
key_points: Omani officials arrived in Tehran Friday for direct Hormuz talks
Iran's and Oman's foreign ministers also spoke by phone
Goal: a mechanism so commercial ships can pass safely
Separately, the US and UK are planning their own Hormuz conference

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil, and a large share of its liquefied natural gas, has to pass through — there's no easy detour. Oman sits at the strait's mouth and, unlike most Gulf states, has kept working relationships with both Iran and the West for decades, making it the natural go-between whenever Hormuz shipping is at risk.

stories.title: India's private-sector growth slows to a 3-year low — but exports are quietly picking up speed
stories.what_happened: The HSBC flash India Composite PMI slipped to 54.3 in July from 57.1 in June — still growth, but the slowest pace in over three years. Manufacturing actually improved slightly, with its output index rising to 57.0 from 56.3, but services — a much bigger share of India's economy — fell sharply to 53.1 from 57.4, its weakest reading in 53 months. Survey respondents cited tougher competition, order cancellations, fewer client enquiries, and shortages of key raw materials. At the same time, new export orders for Indian goods and services grew at their fastest pace since March, driven by strong international demand.
key_points: HSBC flash Composite PMI fell to 54.3 in July from 57.1 in June
That's the weakest private-sector expansion since March 2022
Services activity dropped to its worst reading in 53 months
But new export orders grew at their fastest pace since March

depth.background: The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a monthly survey of manufacturing and services companies about whether business is getting better or worse — a reading above 50 means the sector is still growing, below 50 means it's shrinking. Economists watch it closely because it's available weeks before official GDP data, making it one of the earliest real-time snapshots of how the economy is actually doing.

stories.title: Odds of a surprise Fed rate hike this month triple in a week, as Iran-war oil prices revive inflation fears
stories.what_happened: The probability of a Fed interest-rate hike at the July 28-29 meeting has more than tripled over the past week, rising from about 10.7% to nearly 35-38%, according to the CME FedWatch tool. The jump followed Brent crude oil crossing $100 a barrel for the first time since May, driven by the escalating US-Iran conflict and attacks on Saudi oil facilities. Fed governor Christopher Waller said the Fed would need to 'consider tightening monetary policy in the near term' if another hot inflation reading arrives, while Governor Lisa Cook flagged core inflation already running at 3.7%, nearly double the Fed's 2% target.
key_points: Markets now price roughly a 1-in-3 chance the Fed hikes rates on July 29, up from about 1-in-10 a week ago
Brent crude topping $100/barrel on Iran-war escalation is the main trigger
Fed governors Waller and Jefferson have both flagged they'd support tightening if inflation stays hot
Core inflation is running at 3.7%, well above the Fed's 2% target

depth.background: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is the US central bank — it sets short-term interest rates to try to keep inflation (the rate prices rise) low while keeping the job market healthy. Markets constantly bet on what the Fed will do next using a tool called the CME FedWatch tool, which converts trader bets into implied probabilities. For most of this year, the Fed was expected to hold rates steady or even cut them, since a rate hike makes borrowing (mortgages, business loans, credit cards) more expensive.

stories.title: Ozempic-style drugs keep cutting how much people eat for at least a year, even after hunger comes back
stories.what_happened: A 60-week clinical trial of 120 overweight or obese adults, comparing weekly semaglutide injections plus lifestyle counseling against a placebo plus counseling, found that semaglutide users continued eating 24–30% fewer calories than the placebo group all the way through the final week-60 check-in. Researchers found that the drug's early, sharp reduction in hunger and food-related thoughts partially fades over time — participants reported some appetite returning — but their actual calorie intake stayed persistently lower anyway.
key_points: 60-week trial: semaglutide users ate 24–30% fewer calories than placebo group through week 60
Some early appetite-suppressing effect fades, but the lower food intake mostly sticks
Findings help explain why weight loss on the drug tends to hold up over time
Published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition

depth.background: Semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy) is a GLP-1 drug — a class of medicine that mimics a gut hormone your body releases after eating, signaling fullness to the brain. It has become the most widely used weight-loss and diabetes drug in the world over the past few years, but doctors have debated exactly how its appetite-suppressing effect evolves the longer someone stays on it.

stories.title: Guenther Steiner: Oliver Bearman's Ferrari deal expires this year, and he'll be free to join anyone
stories.what_happened: Guenther Steiner, Haas's former team principal, said publicly that he believes Bearman's contract tying him to Ferrari's junior program will lapse at the end of this year. Because Ferrari has already locked in Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc through 2027, there's no seat for Bearman there. Steiner said that would leave Bearman free to sign with any team — and warned Ferrari it risks losing him to a rival, possibly even Red Bull, if Max Verstappen were to leave that seat open.
key_points: Ex-Haas boss Steiner says Bearman's Ferrari-junior contract runs out in 2026
Ferrari has already committed Hamilton and Leclerc for 2027, leaving no seat for Bearman
Steiner: without a Ferrari seat, Bearman becomes a free agent other top teams can sign
Red Bull reportedly interested, contingent on whether Verstappen leaves

depth.background: Oliver Bearman is a 20-year-old British driver who came up through Ferrari's junior driver program before being promoted to race for Haas (a Ferrari customer team) in Formula 1. He's outperformed his more experienced Haas teammate over the past two seasons and is widely seen as one of the sport's brightest young talents — but his path to an actual Ferrari race seat has been blocked by the team's established, longer-contracted drivers.

stories.title: Trump says Saudi Arabia's new nuclear deal won't take effect until it makes peace with Israel
stories.what_happened: Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that the nuclear deal will only take effect once Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords, saying 'it's time now that they do it.' He acknowledged this isn't likely to happen soon. The condition surprised observers because it wasn't part of the original announcement — the US Energy Department and Saudi government made no mention of an Israel link when the nuclear pact was unveiled.
key_points: Trump added a new condition to the US-Saudi civil nuclear agreement after it was already announced
Saudi Arabia must join the Abraham Accords — the US-brokered pact normalizing ties with Israel
Neither government mentioned this condition when the nuclear deal was first announced this week
Saudi Arabia has long said it won't normalize with Israel without a path to Palestinian statehood, which Israel's government opposes

depth.background: The Abraham Accords are a set of deals, brokered by the US in 2020, in which several Arab countries agreed to formally recognize Israel for the first time. Saudi Arabia — the most influential Arab and Muslim-majority power — never joined, insisting it wants a genuine path to a Palestinian state first. The US and Saudi Arabia recently signed a separate civil nuclear cooperation agreement, letting US firms help build Saudi nuclear power capacity.

stories.title: Iran says it struck US military bases in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan, widening the war
stories.what_happened: Iran's military said it launched a coordinated missile-and-drone attack on US-linked bases across three Gulf-region countries: destroying air-defense and radar equipment in Bahrain, hitting troop and helicopter areas in Kuwait, and striking a jet inside a shelter in Jordan. Iran said the goal was to blind US radar coverage ahead of larger attacks it may still be planning. Washington has not confirmed casualties or damage.
key_points: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it hit US air-defense systems and radar sites in Bahrain
Iran also targeted US-used facilities at Kuwait's Camp Arifjan and other bases
Iran claims it destroyed an F-15 fighter jet inside a shelter at a US base in Jordan
The US has not confirmed any of its facilities or personnel were actually hit

depth.background: The US and Iran have been in an open, undeclared war for weeks: Washington has been bombing Iran's nuclear and military sites, and President Trump has repeatedly threatened a even bigger strike. Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan aren't directly fighting Iran, but they host US troops and bases, which makes them targets whenever Iran wants to hit America without striking US soil directly.

thread.previously: We reported yesterday that Trump signaled a threatened 'massive' US attack on Iran might not be necessary, as Tehran appeared to be getting 'serious' about a deal.
thread.changed: Instead of moving toward a deal, Iran escalated — striking US-linked bases in three Gulf countries at once, which raises the odds Trump follows through on the bigger attack he'd suggested might not be needed.
